speechtext: Are safeguards taken to avoid bankruptcies in the programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and, if so, what are they?

speakeroldname: Hon. lean Marchand (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subtopic: DREE PROGRAMS-BANKRUPTCY SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Yes. Incentive assistance is offered to an applicant only if evaluation by trained professional staff indicates that the proposed project is likely to succeed. Conditions laid down in an offer of assistance are designed in part to ensure that the chances of long-term viability are good. No payment in respect of our offer of incentive assistance is made until an audit and an on-site inspection is made to determine that these conditions are being met. Final payment is made only after a final audit to determine that they have been met during the relevant control period following the point in time when commercial production is achieved. Throughout the process, officers of the Department are available to assist the company with advice that may be helpful in overcoming any difficulties being encountered.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the recently revealed threat to our manufacturing industry, especially the automobile sector, by the disclosure that United States corporations, many of them having branch plants in Canada, have been using the tax deferral program of the United States government for many months, which breaches the spirit and the letter of GATT as well as of the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement, and critically endangers our national economy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 28 TRADE IMPACT OF UNITED STATES DISC PROGRAM ON CANADIAN AUTOMOBILE INDUSTRY AND CANADIAN ECONOMY IN GENERAL
speechtext:
As I indicated a moment ago, the Chair has received notices of motions proposed by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, and the hon. member for Brant. Obviously the matter proposed for discussion by hon. members is one of national interest and importance and it is of concern to members of the House as evidenced by the many questions asked last week.
There are many other factors which the Chair has to bear in mind in considering a proposed motion to adjourn the House. The Chair must be conscious of the provisions of Standing Order 26 and of other practices of the House which determine the manner in which certain questions should be brought forward for debate and the time when such debates can take place. With this in mind it should be noted that two of the notices received are, to some extent at least, in the form of a proposed censure of the government.
I refer in particular to the notice received from the hon. member for Lambton-Kent which proposes to discuss "the failure of the government, as the primary source of knowledge and responsibility in the matter, to inform the House and public whether these reports are true." This would indicate that what is sought by the hon. member is a debate on a motion of censure of the government. I suggest to hon. members that the provisions of Standing Order 26 cannot be invoked for this purpose.
Section 5 of Standing Order 26 specifies that Mr. Speaker shall have regard to the probability of the matter being brought before the House within reasonable time by other means. I remind hon. members that since a motion under Standing Order 26 was submitted and granted early Thursday afternoon, a budget presentation has been announced for next week. The House has also been advised earlier today by the President of the Privy Coun-

cil that the Minister of National Revenue will make a presentation to the House in relation to foreign ownership at five o'clock tomorrow afternoon. I would hope that at least in the case of the budget debate hon. members will have within a reasonable time an opportunity to express views in relation to the matter alluded to in the motions which are now before us. Between now and the close of the current supply period there remain about 40 sitting days. If it is to be assumed that 12 of these days will be used for supply purposes and another six and one-half sittings for the budget debate, it seems to me that ample opportunities will be presented for discussion of matters such as Canada-United States economic relations.
In view of all the circumstances and taking into account the procedural requirements set out in Standing Order 26, the Chair cannot see its way clear to granting these motions at this time.

subtopic: UNITED STATES DISC PROGRAM-MEASURES TO OFFSET EFFECTS-DIRECT REPRESENTATIONS BY GOVERNMENT-RESUMPTION OF GENERAL NEGOTIATIONS

Mr. Speaker, there have been many direct contacts on this subject. I have raised the matter myself on a number of occasions with my United States counter-
May 1, 1972

part, and I know that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has done so with his counterpart in the United States administration. speechtext: Thank you for that very clear and positive answer. subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to continue a debate on a serious matter such as this with the hubbub that usually accompanies the completion of the question period. This problem is not unique to a particular member, since it occurs every day. Probably if I am departing from the Chamber at this time I am as responsible as any other hon. member for some of the noise. I do note, however, that frequently I am, by merely getting to my feet, able to effectively clear the House in short order. I see I have accomplished that today.
I think the Chair will recognize that it is very difficult to take up a continuing story and tie it in with the beginning of the remarks I made just before one o'clock last Friday. For the benefit of those who tuned in late, I feel I should summarize some of those remarks. This is necessary to get people more or less up to date on the remarks I made earlier and to put things into proper context.
On Friday last, following the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), I made some remarks in opposition and in contradiction to their position regarding the retention of the lash. I support that part of the legislation which removes corporal punishment from the Criminal Code. Following the same philosophy, I also oppose the use of the thumbscrew and the rack, on the grounds that indulgence in this kind of brutalization in our institutions does not do a great deal for our attempt to move
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 toward a more civilized reaction to the kind of transgressions which formerly brought about such violence.
I hasten to add that I appreciate and share the repugnance of many people when they learn through the news media of some particular brutal type of crime, such as gang rape, which results in the destruction of the lives of many innocent people. I am not convinced there would be fewer of these crimes if we resorted to more extreme forms of physical punishment. If I were convinced of the deterrent effect, I might take a different view. I recall from my history lessons that once upon a time people were hanged for stealing a loaf of bread, but that kind of punishment has now been abandoned, perhaps on the ground that it did not prevent thievery. I support the motion to change our Criminal Code in respect of what has been traditional in what we called our prison system and which we now refer to as our corrective or rehabilitative institutions.
I appreciate there have been certain views circulated in respect of prison guards and policemen regarding the five-year ban on capital punishment and that there has been a loophole clause which would allow the extreme form of punishment to be applied to capital crimes against police officers, prison guards and officials. I share the concern of the guards and the police officers about the fact that there is no ultimate penalty so they have no protection, or at least less protection than they might have otherwise. There are many arguments pro and con on this matter, but I do not think anyone knows for sure which are right. I would prefer to find myself on the side which suggests that capital punishment is really no deterrent to murder, and that capital crimes would be no less prevalent as a result of a return to capital punishment.
I admit that if I were a policeman and in the position in which three police officers found themselves in the bush near Moncton not more than three weeks ago when they were sent out to arrest an armed man who was suspected of escaping custody, and having been shot at twice from very close range with a shotgun, I would feel perhaps a little bit less responsible about the way in which I apprehended that particular suspect. I can appreciate their feelings, and if I were in that position I think I should be moved to take no chances. I will say nothing else about that matter.
I reiterate and re-emphasize my feeling that a lot of the people who are putting forward the suggestion that we adopt a more repressive kind of punishment for certain individuals are not looking for justice but rather for vengeance. Our courts and our thoughtful social institution personnel should not be concerned with this kind of vengeance. I do not believe that the brutality of corporal punishment in our institutions will have a civilizing effect or will even be a deterrent to these particular wrongdoers, whether they have been convicted of rape or murder. These crimes, for the most part, are not premeditated but are crimes of passion.
I suggested there were three oversights in these amendments to the Criminal Code, and I went into them in some detail. I was disappointed that, although the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) met with representatives at the provincial conference regarding the enshrining of the concept of the right to counsel in our constitution, this amending bill

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 is silent on that subject. I do not think I need say more about that. The fact that it is, I think, speaks for itself. I hope the minister will be moved, when he is considering further amendments to the Criminal Code, to look after this oversight and see that the right to counsel is entrenched, not only in the constitution if we ever ultimately accept one for Canada, but also in the Criminal Code. Many people are being denied their civil rights because they cannot afford counsel to represent them adequately in the courts. If they cannot have this kind of support there will be many occasions on which justice really is not done.
I could go into a long, detailed discussion about my particular views concerning the right to that kind of a voice that is denied people on the ground of their economic situation. I think this is a familiar subject to most people. After all, we have had the Company of Young Canadians, and various other federal programs designed to give a voice to the voiceless. In my opinion, one of the best ways to give a voice to the voiceless is through a public defender system which would provide legal aid, which in most cases now amounts to charity, and would provide a right to counsel before the courts for people who are accused of breaking the laws of our country.
A second subject on which I should like to speak today, and upon which this particular bill is silent is amendments to the habitual criminal section which I believe is section 660 of the Criminal Code. I had hoped that because of representations, I believe by sincere and responsible members of all parties, changes in this section would have been contemplated by the minister. Perhaps the minister is at the moment contemplating a review of this particular section 660 which relates to the habitual criminal, or as it is more commonly known in the correction institutions, the "bitch" section. The reason I make this particular representation is that from time to time I have received letters from various inmates of federal institutions and have also visited those institutions. However, since I refuse to ask the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) for permission to enter a federal institution, I have not darkened the doors of one lately. Anyway, we are still allowed to receive mail from these institutions. This habitual criminal section has been used primarily by only two provinces, British Columbia and Ontario.
The first complaint about this particular section is that a great number of petty criminals, nuisance criminals if you like, are faced with indeterminate or indefinite sentences. There would seem to be an attempt to prescribe an indefinite sentence rather than have the punishment tailored to the crime or have the rehabilitation, if you are looking at the prison system from that point of view, fit the individual. I am afraid it has not worked out in that way in all cases. I am sure it has in a number of cases. A number of people who are serving indeterminate sentences are doing so because they have been convicted of minor, petty or nuisance crimes. I am not saying this is applied exclusively to these people, but there are certainly a great number of them. The result is that those people who have been found guilty of much more serious crimes to person and property have an opportunity which is denied one on a shorter sentence. They are able to enjoy the kind of parole opportunities and temporary absence opportunities which are accorded to prisoners. I believe

this is a source of serious irritation or hostility among those people who have been convicted of less serious crimes to person and property. Right alongside them, they often find persons convicted of a serious crime who have been subject to a more equitable and more enlightened parole system, as well as temporary absence opportunities. That is the basic criticism. I understand the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Hogarth) has made representations on the same subject as a result of his visits. I am not sure his representations would parallel mine and I am aware that he is certainly capable of making a submission on his own behalf. I mention this fact, however, to indicate that there is an expression of concern which extends beyond the voice of one particular member.
There is one further topic in respect of which I wish to indulge myself briefly. It concerns the matter of compensation to victims of crime. Frequently, we learn from news sources that people are amazed that members of society would stand around and watch, without lending a helping hand, while some particular individual is besieged and perhaps harmed physically by the methods used by criminals. One reason I believe goes far beyond the question of not wishing to become involved. There is a real concern on the part of the general public that if a member of the general public were to assist in such a circumstance and should be physically injured himself his own family might suffer as well. The citizen's arrest or the idea of assisting the police I believe has a long tradition in British common law, but is frequently ignored. This tradition I believe is followed more frequently in smaller communities where each person knows everyone as neighbours or friends. However, it is frequently ignored in a city crowd. I believe representations have been made over the years on this subject. I think particularly of the case of a fireman who came to the aid of someone who needed him, whose injury involved a substantial loss of pay.
I notice that the British Columbia legislature recently passed a measure to assist in the compensation of crime victims. So, I put this forward as a little representation for the consideration of the minister. It seems I am always making representations to the minister. I made them in respect of immigration and the lack of reciprocity. Before he could get around to doing something about it, two and a half years later he is not the minister responsible for that department. However, he has listened most attentively. I am sure he has heard these representations and will hear them again. I look forward to him adding this subject to the very progressive bill we have before us.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. B. Osier (Winnipeg South Centre):
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make just one or two short comments. I am very glad to see that at last measures are being taken which, as a non-lawyer, I can only hope will be effective in getting right under the skin of these cancerous individuals who through some warped logic of their own decide it is profitable and fruitful to hijack an aircraft or try to ransom the people on board an aircraft. As I said, I am not a lawyer, but I am very glad to see that the definition of a peace officer includes the pilot of an aircraft when that aircraft is on the ground and when the pilot has taken command of it for the purpose of flying it somewhere. It is my understanding that sometimes the trickiest phase of one
May 1, 1972

of these take-over bids occurs on the ground when peace officers are present.
It is my understanding from talking with pilots that they are very apprehensive about not being in command of the situation until the moment when they want to turn it over to policemen. They have usually had an opportunity of evaluating the mental state of the person who has attempted to hijack the aircraft and they are probably adjusted as much as they can be to the situation. Sometimes, in their opinion, more harm than good can be done by having an over-zealous police force come in with loaded guns and try to solve the situation in a manner with which the pilots probably do not agree. So, I am glad to see that the aircraft will be left in charge of the pilot until such time as he would normally hand it over.
I also have one comment to make about the fact that if a person is found guilty of the indictable offence of hijacking he is subject to life imprisonment. As I understand it, life imprisonment is nothing of the sort. In many cases, it is probably a good thing to allow a person who has been sentenced to life to have his case reviewed, and to be freed after a certain number of years if he has shown signs of penance and a change of heart. However, it seems very difficult to reconcile oneself to the idea that anyone who has hijacked an aircraft should be let out into society again. I cannot understand what kind of egotistical nut could ever think that it was either funny, progressive, amusing or of any value to anyone whatsoever to put the lives of 100 to 200 people in jeopardy. Therefore, I feel that when this bill goes to committee the penalty of life imprisonment should be considered very carefully.
Perhaps psychiatric evidence should be sought to ensure that a person released after a number of years will not be so stupid or so insane as to do the same thing again. It is tragic enough when a man makes another mistake or kills a man after having been let out of prison, but it is about 5,000 per cent more tragic if he hijacks an aircraft and puts the lives of several hundred people in jeopardy. So, I commend the government for having brought these features into the bill. I suggest that when the bill goes to the committee, the committee should ask the Airline Pilots Association to come before it and to give its opinion of the bill. Personally, I would ask the committee to take another good, hard look at the practical result of a sentence of life imprisonment so far as this legislation is concerned.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this omnibus bill is one that permits a wide range of discussion, comprising as it does a multitude of changes in the criminal law. I congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) on the manner in which this whole question has been brought before the House and the degree to which an opportunity is afforded to consider in general, with particular reference to the sections contained therein, the whole problem of the criminal law.
It is on that subject that I intend to speak shortly. I will then refer to two or three matters, all of which have been dealt with before in the debate but on which I will give a somewhat different viewpoint than those already expressed during the course of the debate. I will say
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 immediately that during my years in university and law school, the general feeling was that if only people could live in affluence, most if not all of the problems of mankind would be solved. In the last 50 years, despite the inexcusable poverty which still exists, we in Canada have gone far to bring about one of the highest levels of living in the world. In North America, with reference to the United States and Canada, economic well being beyond imagination at the beginning of this century may well have dulled and even drained away the courage, initiative and vigour of the people. In achieving economic prosperity-and I am speaking about levels of prosperity-are we in danger of losing the spiritual values which nations no less than individuals need to survive?
I was particularly impressed with the speech on the subject by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), who has made a profound study not only of this bill but of criminology in general. It reveals the progress in the House to which he has greatly contributed.
We find that lawlessness has become almost a way of life. Crime is rampant and on the increase in Canada, in the United States and in Great Britain. Why has this come about? Why in Canada last year should almost 5 per cent of our total population find themselves convicted of some offence under the Criminal Code? It is a frightening picture to see that one million Canadians were convicted of criminal offences, and I am not speaking about automobile offences other than manslaughter and that type of offence. The question is being asked: what should be done? Should there be more severe penalties? Has there been too great freedom in the last two or three years in the granting of parole in our country? It was under my administration that the Parole Board was set up, but I was concerned recently when several of those who committed one of the most dastardly offences, that of kidnapping, found themselves released after serving a very short portion of their sentences. That type of thing encourages violence. The violence of a few becomes a contagious disease within our country and other freedom loving countries. One of the reasons is that acts of violence are continually played up in the press, on radio and on television.
There is a movement within our country, as in other western Nations, of an underground nature, the members of which masquerade above ground as crusaders for permissiveness, participate in campaigns for peace, and against the war in Viet Nam. Their leaders claim that what they are doing is an exercise in freedom of speech, when in fact it is often criminal and contrary to several sections of the Criminal Code. Violence begets violence, and unless measures are taken to punish this kind of wrongdoing those who advocate, support and engage in violence will destroy the basis of our democratic society and pave the way for absolute tyranny.
Today we find the youth of our country criticized. I do not join in that. There are 2 or 3 per cent that preach revolution, while the rest want to bring about change by democratic means. Those who pretend that they believe in passive resistance or disobedience as practised by

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 Ghandi, are actually practising revolution and advocating changes in our country on the basis of revolution.
I have stood for the right of the individual to have freedom of speech throughout my life, both at the bar and in the House of Commons. And I have stood for the right of the individual to have that freedom and to advocate the need for change. I believe that impatience, coupled with the will to change, are both needed to bring about orderly progress, but an uncontrolled will to change, practised without restraint, is a menace to freedom. Mob rule is the antithesis of freedom and dare not be condoned if freedom is to be maintained or even to survive. With those few general remarks, Mr. Speaker, I now come to the bill itself.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me dealt with the question of piracy in the air. I brought this matter before the House on March 20 when I asked the minister, as recorded at page 959 of Hansard:
In order to discourage potential hijackers for gain, is the government giving consideration, among other things, to bringing in as part of the de-incentive, if I can use that expression, a provision whereby no airline will be permitted to pay ransom?
The answer was:
There is no immediate intention to introduce legislation along these lines.
I think it should be done, Mr. Speaker. In large measure hijacking is designed to bring about extortion by way of ransom. If the right to extort is denied by law, the incentive to commit hijacking is greatly reduced. I again ask the minister whether he will not give consideration to a further amendment along the line I have suggested here, to the end that we strike at the vital basis for hijacking and kidnapping, except in a very few cases.
There is a strong feeling in certain areas of our country, and among very thoughtful people, that capital punishment should be re-instated. I realize that statistics are always available to prove whatever the person who produces them is endeavouring to prove. But when it is stated that the murder rate is increasing, I do not share that view. What I see is this: that when capital punishment was in effect, if there was any possibility of bringing in a verdict for manslaughter, juries did so. Since the changes have been made in the law removing capital punishment from capital murder, juries today do not have the same qualms about convicting that they used to have. Anyone who has acted both for the Crown and defence knows that if there was a reasonable ground for a jury to find that the accused was not guilty of murder but of the lesser offence of manslaughter, the jury almost invariably took the opportunity of reducing the charge. Everyone is entitled to his or her view of capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, I appeared for the defence many times. Although my experience in criminal law was restricted to about 5 per cent of my total practice at the bar, I defended quite a large number charged with murder. Some wonder why I have such a feeling of concern over the imposition of the death penalty. I ask those who wonder how would you feel if you defended a man charged with murder, who was as innocent as any hon. member in this House at this very moment, who was convicted, whose appeal was dismissed, who was executed; and six months later the star witness for the Crown admitted that he, himself, had

committed the murder and blamed it on the accused? That experience will never be effaced from my memory. The man was so sure he could not be executed that he said to the executioner when he came along to perform the supreme penalty of the law, "You can't hang me; God won't let you." I ask hon. gentlemen to bear that experience in mind when they conclude that those of us who stand against the re-imposition of capital punishment have views that are based on emotion but not on actual experience.
All over the free world capital punishment is disappearing, because we are living in a changing world. My great grandfather saw a boy hanged in Upper Canada for picking pockets in 1837. I think the boy was 17 years of age and everybody gathered for the public execution. Those Scottish people in North York turned up in large numbers. There was a great celebration, and during the ceremonies of the execution four of them had their pockets picked, which just indicates the argument that the fear of capital punishment will greatly reduce the number of offences is not completely tenable, or indeed tenable at all.
I think the record shows that in the United States there has been not one execution in the last three years. Capital punishment has been abolished within the United Kingdom, excepting within those limits which all of us know.
So far as the imposition of the lash is concerned, anyone who has ever seen a man who has been lashed would never advocate the heinous cruelty connected with that operation. It demoralizes not only the individual lashed but also those who have to carry out the penalty.
Next there is the question of common assault and increasing the penalty from a potential two years to five years. I think that is going too far. Common assault can be tried by a justice of the peace. To place in the hands of a justice of the peace the summary right to impose a sentence of from two to five years, is to me inexcusable and unjustified.
The increase in penalties for assault of police officers is, I think, justified on the basis of what too frequently happens today when police officers become a subject of contempt, largely as a consequence of some people referring to them as "pigs". Too often the Canadian who believes in law enforcement fails to give to those same police officers that respect, regard and help which they deserve. Those are just three or four matters to which I wanted to allude.
I wish now to go on to another matter which is not comprised in the bill itself in any way. I am concerned about the fact that we discriminate against the Indian in the administration of law. For many years I was a proponent and advocate of the Bill of Rights which was looked upon in some circles with a certain amount of derision. Many law professors said that it would never be effective. It came into effect in 1960, and for seven long years thereafter various professors and inferior court judges across this country stated that it was in effect a grandiloquent declaration of human rights but would never be effective to protect the rights of the individual.
Then came the Joe Drybones case-a wonderful name that Indian bore. Drybones was found guilty of being
May 1, 1972

drunk in his shack on his reserve. It was an offence under the Indian Act. He was found guilty but he said "You cannot do this to me" and the prosecuting authority said "We have". He appealed and the appeal was allowed. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) had nothing to do with the matter of which I am about to speak, but it has always shocked me that the government of Canada had its counsel argue for a day and a half in the Supreme Court of Canada that the Bill of Rights was not effective and ought not to be declared to be effective. That is what was done by the present government. Pretending to believe in human rights and human freedom, it has its counsel argue in the Supreme Court of Canada with vehemence that the Bill of Rights was a danger to Canada in that it subjected parliament to the surveillance of the courts. The Supreme Court of Canada held, however, regardless of the arguments advanced by the Crown and under the direction of this government now in office, that the Bill of Rights was superior to every law ever passed in Canada since 1867, and where any portion of the statute passed contravened in whole or in part the provisions of the Bill of Rights, to that extent it was a nullity.
Now, a word about the Indians. I always feel a sense of guilt when I see the Indians across our country, who have a right to go into a beer parlour and buy liquor, who have a right to secure liquor from the regular sales outlet, but have no right to have liquor on the reserve. Where are they to consume it? If they consume it on the way home so that they will not break the law on the reserve, they are subject to being charged under the various liquor acts. The fine is usually $50 minimum with the alternative of 30 days in jail. They cannot pay the fine so poverty becomes their passport to prison. That is wrong, Mr. Speaker. In his desire to bring about changes that will ensure human liberty, I would like the Minister of Justice to communicate with the Attorneys General of the various provinces in order to arrive at a plan which will do away with this stigmatization of the Indian.
I visit jails and I see there individuals; decent, responsible, respectable Indians who are unable to pay the fine and are incarcerated because they dared break a provincial law while having been placed in a position where they have no alternative but to break it. If the Minister of Justice were to bring together the various Attorneys General from across the country, I think arrangements could be made to remove this example of discrimination. When it takes place it causes me to have a feeling of revulsion that all who hate injustice would necessarily share. I am not going to speak of what I have done but on more than one occasion, not knowing the individual at all, I have paid his fine so that he would not be incarcerated. That is how strongly I feel on this matter and I hope that the minister, in the spirit in which I advance it, will do his part toward eradicating one of the most serious examples of injustice to an individual which arises because of his colour and by virtue of the fact that he resides on a reservation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to detain the House, but I thought that these few observations might at least start a line of thought that would be beneficial to all of us in that it would ensure justice to all.

speechtext:
Perhaps I can be allowed, however, to correct the right hon. member on an observation that he made in regard to the law proposed by this bill. He suggested that the law is going to be changed so that common assault becomes punishable by five years in prison. I would draw the right hon. member's attention to the provisions of clause 21 of the bill. All that has happened to common assault is that it will be made a summary conviction offence, on which I will comment further in a minute. It is assault causing bodily harm, an indictable offence, where the penalty has been increased to five years. I think this was as a result of a case in the British Columbia Court of Appeal. The Court was limited in the length of the sentence that could be imposed on a particular individual in relation to what they felt was a particularly vicious assault causing bodily harm.
While the field of criminal law is extremely difficult in a modern society, it is especially difficult in Canada where there are different moral standards throughout the country and certainly a conflict between urban and rural societies. The crime rate is up and society is expressing more and more concern. It is difficult to resist the hard line taken by some people. The Chief Justice of British Columbia is alleged to have said "If there is going to be shooting, there will surely be hanging." It is difficult for society to accept the proposition that society's best protection lies in good, sound, modern penology which, in turn, rests on the principles of rehabilitation. We need a police force which is supported by good laws; we need good penology services and we need a good parole service.
We are moving too slowly in the direction of advanced penology in Canada. Although our theories in some instances have not proved too sound, we have made some progress in this area. Nevertheless, we have many years of lag to make up. I notice that the right hon. gentleman pointed out that not until 1958 was our parole board first established. One would think that in a country as modern as Canada such a board would have been established in 1928. Without doubt, harsh measures such as corporal punishment or the noose do not deter violence. Certainly, crimes of violence are on the rise; I doubt very much if we can attribute those to the lack of harsh sentences imposed. I think statistics shortly will reveal that although all crimes of violence are increasing, the crime of homicide, for which in some instances capital punishment has been provided, is showing the slowest rise.

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
So, it would not appear that the noose is a deterrent with regard to offences of that nature. Certainly, public executions are absurd. I understand that public executions were stopped because they became too much of an attraction. Thousands of people would stream to the execution. Instead of executing a man publicly, in recent years the authorities hanged the man in the middle of the night in the privacy and secrecy of a prison. Recently I read a description of a public execution in London, Ontario. That was a disgrace to those times. People had little humanity. Society today would not tolerate such a spectacle. Hanging is not necessary. It is offensive to our basic principles of rehabilitation. I hope with all my heart that all hon. members, in the debate soon to come, will see their way clearly to taking the enlightened point of view.
The actions of the parole board in the case mentioned perhaps could be criticized. Nevertheless, we must remember that the parole board, by and large, hears about 17,000 applications per year and it has done extremely well in discharging its duties. Hopefully, we can extend the parole system beyond its present limits and, by increasing the staff, try to make sure that errors of that sort do not occur. I submit that the behaviour of the inmate during the whole course of imprisonment ought to be the determining factor of his parole. That behaviour pattern could be obtained from an analysis of his day to day conduct. We must also remember, and the minister responsible must take this point of view, that the parole board's function is quasi-judicial. It is not for the politician, it is not for the member of parliament, or for the minister under whose direction the parole board comes, to interfere in any way with the workings of that board or in the manner in which parole is given. If that interference should ever occur, Mr. Speaker, parole would depend upon whom you know, and not on behaviour. As such, the concept will be reprehensible to us all, and I do not think any member of this House would entertain it. By and large, the parole board of this country has done a good job. As I say, I recognize some mistakes it has made. The board will be presenting its estimates before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs tomorrow, and any hon. member who wants to examine a member of the board may do so. Hon. members may examine the board and see exactly what the present situation is and how past mistakes may have arisen or may have been corrected.
I had occasion not long ago to visit the members of the Optimum Club in the maximum security institution in British Columbia, the B.C. Penitentiary. The Optimum Club consists of a group of men, some of whom are serving life sentences of imprisonment-we call them lifers-following conviction under habitual criminal proceedings. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) told us of some of the problems that arise among such sentenced habitual criminals. The problem, really, stems from a change in the judicial interpretation of the law. Some years ago there was a rash of prosecutions under the habitual criminal section and men who had a record of a long string of minor, petty offences were sentenced under the habitual criminal section. Perhaps I am exaggerating the case somewhat. At any rate, those who had been convicted of a long string of minor, petty offences were found to be habitual criminals and were sentenced accordingly.

Today, of course, they are in jail, well knowing that the judicial interpretation of the law which sent them to jail has been changed. Now, only those with a long history of more violent offences are charged as habitual criminals. The members of the club know that if they were to come before the courts today, it is unlikely that they would be convicted of anything more serious than the prime offence, as we call it, which brought about the habitual criminal proceedings. As the hon. member for Fraser Valley West mentioned, I have referred this matter to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and am pleased to note that he is to send the matter to the Law Reform Commission, to be taken up in due course in its deliberations.
So far as habitual criminal proceedings are concerned, may I suggest that the accused be subjected to those proceedings only after he has finished serving his sentence for the prime offence. Only then, after he has finished his sentence for robbery, or whatever he was charged with, should habitual criminal proceedings be undertaken. After that sentence is finished I suggest that he should be placed on life long parole, instead of in a maximum security institution, for a man on lifetime parole would know that if at any time he transgressed the law or the conditions of his parole, he could find himself back in prison. I suggest that would be a better way of treating habitual criminals than incarcerating them, as we now do. Actually, our present habitual criminal proceedings were one of the prime causes of a riot in a British Columbia prison at Oakalla. Some time ago, a number of prisoners charged as habitual criminals were imprisoned in Oakalla. Knowing that they faced a life of perpetual imprisonment if convicted their morale sank so low that they started a riot while awaiting trial.
I want the Minister of Justice, particularly, to pay more attention to what is being said at the grass roots level by those who must administer our bail reform act. I notice that Mr. Stewart McMorran, a name well known to the Minister of Justice and to any Canadian criminal lawyer, has suggested that, in the police courts of Vancouver, the new bail reform act is not working. I think the whole matter of bail reform should be investigated. We must look at this again, or else there will be trouble brewing not only for the minister, but, as well, for the police and authorities who must administer the act.
This bill, an omnibus bill, certainly contains many provisions, some good and some bad. I see, for instance, if I may talk about indemnities for a bondsman, that we are still to prevent professional bondsmen from operating in our cities and communities. This, I suggest, ought to be reviewed. After all, a man charged may be in Montreal, and he may have come, in these days, from Winnipeg, Calgary or any other city in Canada. When charged he may find himself in Montreal; also, the reverse may be true. That man may not be able to get bail because he has no friends in Montreal. From my experience, it is difficult to put up property as bail; if the property is much more than a half mile away, so to speak, there are great difficulties. I hope that provision will be made for professional bondsmen. I see nothing wrong with this. Professional bondsmen have been excluded under our criminal law because, under the old common law concept, a man's friends were the ones who would get him back to court if he was reluctant to face justice. I think in modern society
May 1, 1972

that basic concept has become outworn. A professional bondsman, after he has been thoroughly investigated, ought to be acceptable. I hope this bill will include provisions to that effect.
The provisions with respect to soliciting for purposes of prostitution are somewhat obscure. It is interesting to note that prostitution never was an offence. I do not think that prostitution has ever been an offence in the history of the common law or our statute law. Incidentally, offences pertaining to prostitution have. We now come to the part dealing with soliciting and I quote:
Every person who solicits any person in a public place for the purpose of prostitution-
I do not know what it means to solicit for the purpose of prostitution. Does it mean that someone is going to try to induce someone to become a prostitute? However, it appears some dressing up has to be done with that clause. Why not go the whole way and say that any person who is found with a prostitute is also guilty of an offence? Why not be honest about this, and say that if prostitution is against the law in any way, those who use prostitutes are also committing an offence. But oh, no, this is a very masculine society. I should not say that because this provision now applies to both men and women. I will comment on that in a minute. Nonetheless, the predominant use of prostitutes is by men. If we are going to deal with prostitution in any way, shape or form, those who participate should be just as guilty as those who are prostitutes.
Today is a day of come-uppance. During the course of the debate on the omnibus bill when we amended the section of the Criminal Code dealing with indecency, I drew to the attention of the justice committee and the solicitors who were present from the Department of Justice that if we were going to permit gross indecency in private, we would have to amend the law pertaining to male prostitutes. I was assured that the law, as it then read in the Criminal Code, was quite satisfactory. It gives me great pleasure to draw to Your Honour's attention the fact that clause 14 of this bill now does exactly what I said should have been done three years ago, after several judges in this country pointed out to the Crown the essence of their stupidity.

I have a lot of views about that. I am concerned. The repeal of the law pertaining to vagrancy is discomforting. Common law offences relating to vagrancy were codified in our Criminal Code as early as the 1898 version. The trouble with the offence of vagrancy is there is one catch-all section which deals with the person who has no apparent means of support. Section 175(1) reads:
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
Every one commits vagrancy who
(a) not having any apparent means of support is found wandering abroad or trespassing and does not, when required, justify his presence in the place where he is found;
That section was of tremendous use in law enforcement. When someone was found in a dark alley hiding behind a telephone pole or a garage and watching a dwelling house, a policeman could take that man into the police station and legitimately ask him what he was doing. This section does not apply now, other than the one Part dealing with a dwelling house and, I should specifically put the case in a warehouse district to get it more clearly established. Such a person can now stay there, drift into the darkness and rob the warehouse in the next block. The time has come for some policemen to obey the law, although I do not suggest that they do not now do that. We have good law enforcement people. However, in order to make sure the policemen are protected when they act, there should be a section enabling them to remove people when circumstances indicate they are obviously on the verge of committing an offence. We better look at that carefully when the bill is in committee.
I am glad the law officers of the Crown have advised the minister to go as far as including the offence of canoeing while impaired. Our impaired driving sections have been applied to vessels. Assuming a canoe is a vessel, I can visualize someone cruising down the river while his ability to paddle is impaired by alcohol.
There will be a particularly good debate on this. The breathaliser section, under which the Canadian public were promised the accused would receive a sample of his breath, is in this bill. A sample of breath can be taken by the police but, of course, nothing whatsoever has been done to provide a suitable container to give the accused a sample of his breath. It is just put in there for political window dressing to fool the Canadian public into thinking we are great reformers, thinking only of their interest. Everyone knew this at the time that section was put in the bill, and I drew to the attention of the committee the fact that there was no such thing as a container in which a sample of a person's breath could be retained for the purpose of measuring the alcohol content. I understand there is still not one available. Now, the same provision is included in the section covering the offence of canoeing while impaired. This nonsense should stop until such time as we get a proper container. Perhaps I am prejudging the case. Maybe the minister has one in his pocket which he will bring to the committee. I look forward to being the first to test it.

The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to common assault. Common assault was previously one of the few offences which could be proceeded with either by way of summary conviction or indictment. Impaired driving and dangerous driving are the others. The value of having this as an indictable offence was that it often came in handy in jury trials. If a jury wanted to convict a man of an offence, but not manslaughter, assault causing bodily harm, wounding or maiming, the judge could direct them that common assault was an included offence in the indictment. It is
1776

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 now a summary conviction offence. It cannot be included in a proceeding with an indictable offence. Often the jury compromised on a verdict and the man was dealt with much more lightly than he would have been in the first instance.
With regard to the offence in clause 27 on page 18 of the bill, having in one's possession a motor vehicle with the serial number obliterated, the onus should be on the Crown to prove the accused knew it was obliterated. It should not be left the way it is now.
I am concerned about the provision in clause 38 which appears on page 24 of the bill. This provision permits a justice, acting under that part of the Criminal Code, to remand an accused, and I quote:
for a period not exceeding thirty days without having heard the evidence of a duly qualified medical practitioner where he is satisfied that compelling circumstances exist for so doing and that such a medical practitioner is not readily available to examine the accused and give evidence;
With the greatest of respect, medical practitioners are the last persons who like to appear in court. I am afraid that where you have an accused who may appear to be a little dull, but certainly has all his marbles if I may use that expression, remanding him for 30 days will be a good excuse for police officers who prosecute in rural communities to imprison him when he otherwise would have been brought to trial. The medical facilities in this country are adequate and the provision that the remand must be on the evidence of a medical practitioner should be retained. In any event, we look forward to hearing the minister with regard to that particular clause and the reason for the change.
Finally, I wish to speak about the concept of conditional discharge which appears at page 33 of the bill. This will now be possible under section 662.1 of the code. It is grossly inconsistent. I am not in favour of the conditional discharge concept. The British had a conditional discharge some years ago, but they repealed it. It is no longer in their law. We are rather far behind in law reform and will have to go through that period of experience before eventually throwing it out. It is incongruous. I quote:
Where an accused, other than a corporation-
Why they should be exempt is beyond me. In any event, if he pleads guilty or is found guilty of an offence, the court may, instead of convicting him, place him on probation. In short, he is on probation for an offence of which he was never convicted, and that is surely nonsense. When an accused pleads guilty, or is found guilty, then he is convicted. That is precisely what has happened to him. I would much prefer that the minister consider that a magistrate or a judge has the right, having heard all the evidence against the accused, to decide that it is not in the interests of the community in which the accused lives-or in the interests of justice, if I may put it in that way-to convict him. He has heard all the evidence but he makes no finding. In cases of guilty pleas perhaps exceptions could be made or some qualifications attached.
A prime example of what I mean is women who have reached the menopause period of their lives and the strain is such that they sometimes become shoplifters. This sit-

uation is well known in the courts, and certainly these women should not be convicted of such an offence. They pick a load of groceries and walk off with it because they are mentally deranged. This sort of thing has happened to many women. Similarly, there are men who should not be convicted of certain offences, depending on the individual case. In such cases, I suggest the magistrate should have the right to say that it is not in the interests of justice that the case proceed and that he will enter a stay of proceedings. The attorney general has this right. In any proceeding his agent, the Crown prosecutor, may tell the clerk of the court without leave that he wants to enter a stay of proceedings in a certain case, and then that case is over, unless he wants to proceed with it at a later date.
We are now making provision for this in the bill with regard to summary conviction offences. This is the sort of thing a court should be allowed to do because then there is no conviction. Perhaps there should be special provision made in the case of a guilty plea where a magistrate has the power to hear representations from the accused or his representative to set aside the guilty plea and to enter a stay of proceedings. In that way, we would be able to circumvent the absolute garbage we find in the bill that would result in placing on probation an accused who pleads guilty without convicting him. I suggest this is a matter we should look into during the committee hearings. I am a little surprised we have not sought to benefit from the English experience and dress the bill up properly in the first instance.
I am extremely proud to be in a parliament where we are moving toward the abolition of corporal punishment. I must say to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) that no member has done more than he to insist that the government get down to this question. I remember debating a private member's bill that he introduced on this subject a couple of years ago. Other hon. members have also supported this proposal. Corporal punishment is a most demoralizing thing to men in prison when you are trying to convince them that the "Catch 22" of crime is a change of attitude toward their fellow man and society. The way out of jail for them is a change of attitude. It is the only way out, and if they do not change their attitude in prison then it will not be long before they are back again.
Just what is it that happens when you put a man in a room, take the skin off his back with the cat-o-nine tails, then take him back to his cell, as they used to-though I do not know what is the procedure now-and throw salt water on the wounds? The attitude the other prisoners have to that sort of treatment is: "That is the way that society treats the likes of us". They identify very closely in the prison subculture. This is why seeing this type of nonsense eliminated gives me great pleasure, and is a reward to the hon. member to whom I have referred for his insistence. Your Honour will note that in the justice committee the other day the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) said that corporal punishment would never be used in prisons so long as he was minister. Prison wardens or custodial officers are finding that they can get along without its use, that they do not need it any more. Isolation is one of the remedies being substituted for corporal punishment.
May 1, 1972

I am looking forward to the bill going to committee and, hopefully, getting the law officers of the crown to change their views here and there on the bill where perhaps they are wrong. I am looking forward to participating with other hon. members in the deliberations of the committee on what will be a very interesting experience in the criminal law.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was, as I am sure were others, very interested to listen to the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth), especially to his careful and incisive analysis of the poor wording in some of the clauses of the bill, which presumably reflects his opinion of the poor advice given by law officers of the Crown. It is not very often that we get hon. gentlemen so closely attached to the government itself giving an indication that perhaps the consideration and advice given by law officers, who I take to be the lawyers in the Department of Justice who do the drafting and give legal advice to the Crown,'has'been poor.
We all know that the hon. member has tremendous ability and mentality to be able to see through a lot of this bad advice, and I am sure we will all remember this in future if and when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) gets up on a major point and indicates that he got advice from the law officers of the Crown regarding a certain way to proceed. It puts the thing in proper perspective and probably indicates that, on a number of occasions in the past when hon. gentlemen in government have risen to endorse their position by resting upon the sanctity of the law officers of the Crown, they have been given bad advice and have accepted it. So far as the operation of government is concerned, this is probably a bad thing. However, I do not want to go too far in that direction, except to say that it was interesting to hear some hon. member opposite finally admit in this House that bad advice is sometimes given, and perhaps has been given in the case of this particular bill.
I suppose we cannot very well, and should not, approach any bill relating to the criminal law of the country by looking at the criminal law alone to see what it is that the government proposes to change, to add or to take away. We have at the same time to look at the effect that the law has on individuals who appear before the courts charged with some offence against the law, and see what might be the outcome for the individual. In other words, not only should we be considering the rights of individuals and property offended against; we must also look at the possibility of rehabilitation, so-called, of the individual who offends against the law. There is a companion attitude that we have to take in this connection. This has been reflected in the comments of many hon. members who have wondered about the effectiveness of the law as it is applied to individuals who offend the law, and as to whether or not there will be remedial or preventative steps taken, so far as that same individual or some other individual is concerned, to prevent infractions of the law in the future.
I do not say this from having made a study of it, not being involved in the legal profession in any way, but it appears that the Criminal Code is concerned almost
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 exclusively with offences against people and property, whether they be ones of individual injury, such as might be the case in an assault, or ones of theft, in the case of break and entry or something of that sort. That is about all that is of concern to the Criminal Code itself. There is a companion part which would seem to be based on the theory of deterrence. In other words, we seek to create an offence and bring some punishment to bear upon anyone who is convicted of committing that offence, the theory being that if the punishment is severe enough it will deter that person from committing that or similar offences in the future, or if it becomes public knowledge that the punishment is severe there will be a spin-off effect deterring other people from committing an offence against the law. In other words, if we make the punishment severe enough this will stop crime. I do not think that is true to the extent we seem to think it is.
It has been stated on many occasions, and I think this is an over-simplification, that we have an 80 per cent recidivism rate in our federal penal institutions. In other words, as I understand it, 80 per cent of the people who are in federal prisons today have been in jail before at some time during their lives, some once, some innumerable times, some in provincial jails and others only in federal institutions. If the theory of deterrence, upon which the criminal law in part is based, were fully effective, then presumably in theory a person might commit only one offence and then be deterred by the severity of the punishment from committing any further offences, and others, knowing what punishment is likely to be handed out, would not commit an offence in the first place. That is pretty false reasoning and should not have, to the extent it does, any place in the development of criminal law. We should not try to develop criminal offences, a criminal code and criminal law with that concept in mind. We should have some other type of concept in mind, namely what can we do to assist the individual who offends against the law in order that he will not repeat his actions?
What can we do to establish social concepts or an attitude about offences against persons and property so that those who have not committed any offence will not do so because they consciously desire not to rather than because of fear of punishment? In a number of instances, the side notes in the bill use the word "punishment" to indicate what will be visited upon an individual if he is convicted of theft, or whatever the offence may be. Reference is made to the terms of punishment and injury to the individual who has injured somebody else. It reflects the concept of retribution and revenge, which is different from the question of deterrence, although that is wrapped up with it.
I think probably we still have a carryover within our general attitude about these matters which reflects a bit of the past and carries with it a concept of punishment, which history has shown to be not acceptable. We still say to ourselves that even though we do not have any vengeful feelings, we intend to punish somebody or wreak vengeance upon him for something he has done to somebody else. In the process of doing this, we hope to deter that person and others from comitting offences in the future.

Apropos of that, I should like to make a comment about the law relating to murder. For almost five years now we have had a law which provides that if a person is convicted of murdering a police officer or a penitentiary guard, I think those are the two classes, that is capital murder and the person convicted of committing such an offence will be hanged. In all other cases, the individual will not be hanged. I have expressed my views as to whether or not that type of penalty is a deterrent to a person committing that offence, and hope to have the opportunity to do so again when this subject comes up again for discussion. To the extent that people feel the threat of hanging is a deterrent to individuals to commit murder of a police officer or a prison guard, the whole concept is being negated by the government itself. If parliament has said that in these cases where someone has murdered a police officer or a penitentiary guard that person shall be hanged, I do not think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or anybody else has the right to thumb his nose at the law of the land as expressed by parliament. The government should not say it does not care what parliament has said or what the law is because the government is supreme.
I do not know how many cases there have been in the past few years, and four or five come to mind quickly, where a police officer has been murdered and an individual convicted, the sentence imposed by the court but set aside primarily because of the attitude of the Prime Minister. To the extent that you accept the idea that capital punishment is a deterrent, this action on the part of the government entices people to commit murder of police officers and penitentiary guards. If the deterrent concept has any value whatsoever, the government has removed that value because those who are involved in circumstances, for whatever reason, leading to the murder of a policeman or penitentiary guard do not think in terms of automatically being hanged since the government continues to commute their sentences. The deterrent to that extent is removed. I do not think it should be considered in the first place because I do not buy the idea, but so long as it is in existence it should be respected. I hope the minister is not shaking his head in disagreement with the force of what I have said. When such a person as the Prime Minister brings the law of the land into disrepute by ignoring and thumbing his nose at it, he entices others to do the same thing.
The criminal law also rests on the concept of establishing the punishment to fit the crime rather than taking into account the individual who may be charged with the commission of an offence. This situation is changing. The courts, in some instances, are becoming more enlightened and concerned about the individual and less concerned about making the punishment fit the crime. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth) referred in general to the case of a woman reaching the age of menopause, being emotionally disturbed by that process and engaging in shoplifting. He suggests this should not be considered an offence, in the normal sense of the word, against the criminal law.
As I understood him, he said that in many cases the Crown prosecutor will simply ask the court clerk to enter a stay of proceedings, in other words not proceed further

with the case, because there is a recognition of the possibility of an individual technically committing an offence of theft or whatever the charge for shoplifting is. This situation is changing. A different sort of attitude is developing. We have the opinions of psychiatrists, for what they may be worth, and quite frankly I do not think much of them in many of these cases; but in many respects these opinions are being heeded by the courts. However, we still have the general problem of fitting the punishment to the crime. The operation of the Parole Board is supposed to alleviate the force of the law as it is vented upon someone who has committed an offence. In theory, the Parole Board is supposed to look at these individuals who are in jail and say they do not have to serve their time in jail but can part of it outside. This shows a concept of concern for the individual.
I quite frankly think that the Parole Board, while it operates in this area of lessening the impact of the punishment in terms of time spent in jail, none the less is a highly conservative structure. It may be highly conservative because of the nature of the Parole Act which set up the board, but none the less it is conservative. Of course, one must be selective in this procedure and this is where the decision-making comes into it. But I advance the idea that in many instances the very best time at which to give a person a parole is on the day he is sentenced by the court, especially in cases where a person has been convicted of a crime arising out of an emotional involvement. A person may be emotionally unbalanced at the time of committing a murder because his or her spouse has been involved in some extramarital relations with someone else and has been discovered in that act. In such situations, the result is usually an offence of murder and the likelihood is that the individual involved will not again run into a similar circumstance. It is not a deliberate act or an act of a criminal nature such as a bank robbery. For a person of that type to have to spend 5, 6 or 7 years in jail, or some period of that nature, before some favourable consideration may be given to him by the Parole Board is really stretching the point. To the extent that we want to buy the idea of balancing out the punishment concept by the use of the Parole Board, I think the Parole Board could operate in this area and be a little more generous in its consideration of these cases.
Another matter with which I think we must concern ourselves arises when we come to the matter of the punishment fitting the crime versus the punishment so-called-and I place that in quotation marks-fitting the individual. This comes into focus when we talk about the disparity in sentencing. We know of instances where a person who commits an offence in one jurisdiction may receive a pretty severe sentence from one judge or one court, either because that judge has an apoplectic view about that type of crime or a certain concept of punishment and deterrence, or because of local situations which might exist which may influence the court or judge either consciously or unconsciously. On the other hand, a person in similar circumstances in another part of the country may commit an identical offence and receive either a suspended or very light sentence, or a stay of proceedings, or whatever result the court or Crown may wish to secure.
Inasmuch as the Parliament of Canada is reviewing the criminal law for all of Canada, I do not think we should
May 1, 1972

permit such wide disparities to exist in various parts of the country that one person may receive a ten-year sentence for the theft of $201, while another person may receive a one-year sentence for the theft of $50, $60, $70 or $100 in some other part of the land. Surely, there ought to be an attempt to bring sentencing into some balance, so that all persons have a relatively equal chance to obtain the same consideration in a court no matter in what part of the country they may happen to be. I do not know whether or not this can be accomplished by the process of drawing people into the courts who are in the probationary field or people who may want to help others over a rough period. We do not know whether or not that sort of approach would work. I do not believe we have had sufficient experience in Canada to say it would, but certainly it would be far better to try a procedure of that sort than to allow the sentencing procedure to operate as it has in the past.
If I may, I should also like to mention the question of writs of assistance which are not really a part of the criminal law as such. There is no provision for them within the Criminal Code. However, they are, in effect, search warrants given to peace officers. Two, three or four laws of parliament such as the Narcotic Control Act, the Customs and Excise Act and the Food and Drug Act provide for writs of assistance to peace officers. Writs of assistance are probably not well known outside this House or outside of people who have been on the receiving end of them. Basically they give a police officer the right to enter premises, to break in doors, to search premises and arrest people at any time of the night or day. In other words, a writ of assistance is a blanket sort of search warrant to break into premises, search for whatever is wanted and arrest people without having a warrant, simply on the grounds of suspicion.
Writs of assistance are considered by the Bar Association to be offensive and against the concept of the rights of individuals. I spoke with the former Minister of Justice about this matter when writs of assistance were used by police officers to invade the premises of a number of people in a very small community in northern British Columbia last year. We raised the matter on another occasion when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister when writs of assistance were used to invade the homes of thousands of people of Chinese origin in this country who saw their papers and everything of a documentary nature seized. When I spoke to the previous Minister of Justice about this, he said he would be removing it but the only thing that has been removed has been the former Minister of Justice. I would certainly think, at a time when some kind of an over-all approach to criminal law is being taken in this bill, although it is not as wide and all-encompassing as we would have liked to see it, there should be a new approach taken to writs of assistance because of the fact they offend against the rights of individuals and in many cases are misused.
The habitual criminal sections, on which I would like to comment, should be removed from the criminal law because, even though there has been a variance in the interpretation and application of the provision over the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 years, they offend against our fundamental rights in two ways: one, they impose a second sentence on a person for something for which a court has already convicted and sentenced him, and second, they impose a sentence on the individual because of the belief that in the future he may commit some criminal offence. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth) said, this section was used extensively. It was used in Vancouver by Stewart McMorran, who was at that time Crown prosecutor and who saw an excellent opportunity from his point of view to lodge all drug addicts in penitentiaries in the lower mainland for the rest of their lives. Some 15 years ago or so, he took occasion to proceed against nearly every drug addict who had been convicted of three indictable offences since the age of 18, most of them for possession of narcotics, through the use of the habitual section. Dozens of them were classified as habitual criminals and lodged in jails for the rest of their natural lives.
I do not support the idea advanced by the hon. member for New Westminster that once a person has concluded the sentence for an offence for which he was convicted he should then be on parole for the rest of his life. If you apply the same reasoning to everybody who has been convicted of any offence, every such person could be on parole for the rest of his life. Presumably this would empty the jails. In any event, it still carries with it the concept of the imposition of additional punishment on an individual for something for which he has served his sentence, and also imposition of punishment into the future for an offence that he might commit. This is crystal ball gazing and is just as offensive as the provision in the bill presently before us.
There is a provision in the bill relating to the Criminal Records Act. Inasmuch as we have opened it up, I would advance another thought with respect to it, one that we advanced when the criminal records bill was before the House a few years ago. Under the act at present a person who receives a pardon under the Criminal Records Act is free from questioning by an employer as to whether or not he has been convicted of a criminal offence for which he has or has not been pardoned. This is only applicable in those employer-employee relationships that come under federal parliamentary jurisdiction. It does not apply to companies operating purely within the provincial field. So any employer who comes under provincial jurisdiction, not the federal labour code, may seek to ask any person who has been given a pardon whether in fact he has been pardoned and whether in fact he has been convicted of a criminal offence. That sort of query offends against the moral force of the Criminal Records Act. Inasmuch as we are dealing in the field of criminal law, which parliament has the right to do under the constitution, we should not hide behind the BNA Act which prohibits us from intruding into employer-employee relationships in the provincial field. If it is valid to say to companies operating under the federal jurisdiction that the state has given a person this pardon and the employers cannot inquire as to whether or not he has a pardon, we should say the same thing to all companies operating under provincial jurisdiction and give to the individual to whom the state has already given the pardon the full benefit of protection throughout his time of potential employment.
