May I conclude by commenting, as did the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), on the law as it applies to the Indian people. We are in agreement that perhaps the law itself is not so much discriminatory as is the attitude of some courts, some sections of our society and perhaps some members of the police force as well. The Prince Albert penitentiary with which the right hon. member is familiar-at least from the outside, I do not think he has been inside the institution to visit it- contains a population 50 per cent of which is Indian. I heard some statistics the other day, related to me by an individual who said that they had been compiled by someone else, which showed that of the 20,000 people in jail in Canada today-obviously this includes provincial jails as well-60 per cent are Indian or of Indian descent. It is a shocking state of affairs when one considers that the population of Indians as related to the total in Canada is somewhere in the neighbourhood of one per cent or one and a half per cent.
Surely, there is something wrong in the attitude towards the Indian people when we see this great preponderance in terms of percentage end up in our jails. Surely, it cannot be entirely the fault of a group of people classified as Indians that a high percentage of them have greater criminal tendencies than the rest of the population. Surely, that cannot be the inference drawn from these statistics. It is certainly not my thought, and I am sure that anybody who looks at this in a reasonable way would reach the same conclusion. One must also conclude, by the same token, that there is something wrong with the system, the attitude, the administration of justice, and the imposition of punishment by the courts on Indian people who appear before them. As I stated, the Prince Albert penitentiary is half filled with people of Indian ancestry. There is a feeling among many Indian people that the law discriminates against them, and I think it has proven to be the case in some instances.
In the Cariboo area of British Columbia a few years ago, I have forgotten the precise circumstances relating to the situation, an Indian girl had been attacked by some so-called white men. I think she died as a result, although I may be mistaken. As the result of the attack that took place-and I think rape was involved and a variety of pretty heinous activities-the individuals were convicted and received an insignificant sentence, one of them a fine and a couple of years in jail or something like that. We all know that if that situation had been reversed, if it had been a couple of Indian boys who had engaged in the same activities with a white girl, there would have been one hell of a hue and cry for a hanging to take place. But it did not.
I know of an occurrence which took place in another part of British Columbia 15 years ago when a chap was with a young Indian girl. I suppose there was drinking involved, I am not sure of that, but in any event he proceeded to attack her physically. He put the boots to her, and as a result she rolled down some stairs in a rooming house; in effect, he killed her in the process of assaulting her with his boots. He got four years, Mr. Speaker. Just reverse that situation and imagine the result if that had been an Indian lad who did that to a white girl! There would not have been any four years involved. There would have been a hue and cry for a

hanging of that individual, or a long sentence at the very least, with lashes.
The Fred Quilt affair, I submit, is another case in point. These are ones I know of because they relate to my own province, but you can duplicate this situation in other provinces. Here is another case in point where there is, to be overly generous about it, a convinced attitude on the part of the Indian people in British Columbia that a crime had been committed by a member of the RCMP, and it had been whitewashed. The extremely generous would say that, but this is a situation which took place. This confirms once more that Indian people are discriminated against in their relations with the law. Just a few years ago we had a federally appointed commission on the law and the Indians. It came up with a number of opinions, views and recommendations on courses of action that should be taken. For a few years, we persistently asked what the government was going to do with respect to that report, and the answer we always got from the government benches was, "It has nothing to do with us. It is not our responsibility. Under the constitution, the administration of justice comes under the provinces." They completely wiped their hands of the whole system. They completely ignored the validity of the points made by that commission.
Is it any wonder that there is an attitude that, yes, the law discriminates against the Indians? Is it any wonder an attitude exists that, yes, the white man discriminates against the Indians, since they are on the receiving end every time they come up against the law? It is a shameful commentary if in this day and age we have to stand up in this House of Commons, and admit that such things do exist. It is a very shameful thing for people in parliament to have to admit, but it is a fact. This situation does exist and it needs correcting, as do many of the other abuses that prevail with respect to the application of criminal law against individuals who have committed offences against persons or property but who are not given the other side of the coin, namely, help from society which will rehabilitate the individual who commits the offence.
I doubt that these matters will be cleared up when the bill gets before the committee. I hope they will be cleared up, but I doubt it very much. We know that this is not the bill of the current Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). He did not conceive it. He did not develop it. It is an inheritance, a legacy from his predecessor. I do not say this unkindly, but this is the normal case with such legislation. But I do hope that he, being a person learned in the law, being a human sort of person with his feelings about people, would take to heart not only what I have said but what members of his own party and other parties have said, so that when he appears before the committee he will not simply be trying to defend the wording of the bill before us, he will not simply be trying to adjust a few words here and there to meet some insignificant objections to the bill, but rather will approach it from the point of view of trying to do something worth while for the total population.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH CENTRE TO CO-ORDINATE STUDIES OF WORLD PROBLEMS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider, in furtherance of the objectives of the United Nations, the establishment and operation in Canada of a world centre to program and administer co-operation between and co-ordination of the efforts of experts and institutions in their studies of compelling world issues respecting (a) international relations and peace (e.g. problems of peace-keeping, 'farms control and disarmament, human rights and intercultural communications) (b) global problems of development (e.g. the use of natural resources, international trade and problems of developing economies, transfers of science and technology, population problems and concerns of youth) (c) the environment and, in particular, the impact of science and technology on the environment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion is self-explanatory and I do not plan to use all the time allotted to me because I would like to hear the views of other hon. members of this House. I also hope that there might be unanimous consent to dispose of this motion, either by referring it to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence or by passing it.
The concept of a world university does not originate with me but has been suggested on a number of occasions by the largest volunteer organization in this country, the Canadian Home and School and Parent-Teacher Federation. This is a very important association concerned with the greatest activity that takes place in this country, apart from government, the business of education. Since 1965, the Canadian Home and School Association, through a special committee, has given a great deal of attention to the concept of an educational institution which would help to alleviate much of the misunderstanding and dissension that creates at times almost impossible barriers against the solution of international problems. I can recall correspondence with the association as far back as 1967 to the effect that it would be a most appropriate gesture in that centennial year if we could establish a world university so that our celebrations would not merely be selfindulgent but would make a contribution to the larger constituency and larger neighbourhood of the world itself.
I think it is fair to say that in 1967 and shortly afterwards, the possibility of using the Expo site for a world university was discussed. It is a little ironical that the matter was never given serious consideration, and that in recent years the city of Toronto has indicated a strong interest in establishing a world university there. Perhaps this just illustrates the continuing conflict and competition between Toronto and Montreal; the compromise might be to locate such a university in Prince Edward

May 1, 1972
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study Island, but I shall refrain from that kind of parochial comment.
The basic concept is well worth consideration because there are any number of initiatives that a country like Canada should take in the interests of international cooperation. We have taken some excellent initiatives in the past, and undoubtedly one of the most important has been the recognition of Mainland China and the impact of that decision at the United Nations and in the United States of America. There are others of which we have been most neglectful, such as our recent peacekeeping attempt and humanitarian attempts with respect to the civil war in Nigeria and our approach on questions related to development in the third world. While we have made many excellent speeches on this second matter, there has been little evidence that we are prepared to take this kind of development seriously.
One thing is clear: we have to gear our response to the challenge of international co-operation to the resources we have available, both material and intellectual. It is naive to suggest that we can only respond to the call for international co-operation on a plane of basic self-interest because the whole question of self-interest can be defined in many ways. It is my view that Canadians have had and continue to have very deep interest in events that transpire beyond our borders. Only last night, when observing the National News I was intrigued to note that our public broadcasting system featured six or eight news items from other parts of the world before turning its attention to domestic activities. This means that there is a very real interest, and a sense of responsibility in this country, about what is happening abroad. It is not necessary to list those who have contributed time and talent to a host of international agencies. We do this not only from a humanitarian concern but because we realize that we do not live in some kind of isolated existence. I think it was Barbara Ward or Buckminster Fuller who said that we are really together in this fragile spaceship, earth, and that what happens halfway around the globe will have a challenging effect on our country.
The purpose of this motion is to establish that we believe that international co-operation is not some kind of abstract goal, but that it is a very real tool toward the resolution of real problems facing the international community. We are saying through this motion that Canada wants to go on record as offering a mechanism for the international study and resolution of problems that affect all citizens of the world. It is really not appropriate for national communities or countries of the world to develop totally independent approaches to international problems and then hope for some miraculous capacity for independent solutions to blend into one common resolution of the problem.
I think we have already seen how this kind of isolated approach to complex international issues makes it difficult to find some kind of consensus. If the problem is a common one, as is pollution, for the entire developed world, then common priorities and critical procedures must be developed. Within a month or two the first world conference on the environment will be held in Stockholm; but one conference in a fairly formal setting with papers being presented will not move us much closer to the

problems that are rapidly developing in the environmental field unless we have a continuing framework within which these issues can be faced and resolved or positions put forward whereby the responsible agencies of government can give them full consideration. I believe the common priorities and critical procedures must be developed. Common information must be available and common resources must be mustered in the battle. Narrow national solutions will remain just that, narrow and limited in scope and effectiveness. I think it is clear that narrow solutions are no longer acceptable or even feasible from a political or economic or even environmental point of view. We have to develop new procedures and new opportunities for the resolution of these problems.
As recently as a few days ago, Mr. John E. Ricketts who has been giving leadership to the international committee of the Canadian Home and School and Parent-Teacher Federation, upon being notified of the motion placed on the order paper, sent the following letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp):
Knowing that this federation has been actively promoting the idea of a world university, preferably but not necessarily in Canada, since 1965-
He goes on to commend the motion that I have proposed, and then continues:
In view of the communications we have exchanged with your department in recent years, you will know that this federation warmly supports the motion, and hopes that the government will act on it.
U Thant's 1969 suggestion for a United Nations international university comes before the General Assembly for the third time- and probably for the decisive vote-this fall. The aim of UN U would be to work with existing universities in all countries to unite the world's academic resources in co-operative search, in a nonpolitical setting, for solutions to world problems.
All UN member nations, and the university community at large, were invited to express views on the idea. Our last information was that most of the emerging nations have indicated strong approval, but that Japan is the only advanced industrial nation to have done so.
The threats to world existence-from pollution, misuse of natural resources, weapons of mass destruction-have never been more obvious. This Federation again urges the Government to give full support to the proposed United Nations University.
I think it is clear from Mr. Ricketts' latest letter that this will be a crucial and deciding vote later this year. Of course, I am speaking of the vote concerning the matter of the United Nations University. It is sad, even tragic, that the government has not yet indicated its position on the proposal that has been before the United Nations for the past three years. Although United Nations officials to whom we have talked would welcome enthusiastically the support by our country for this concept, that does not mean that we must necessarily become involved in the matter of the location of that United Nations University.
Of course, my motion expresses the hope that Canada may provide the site. I am in favour of that possibility not only because I am Canadian, and in that sense I may be said to express a parochial point of view, but, as well, for another reason. Having visited people in other countries and travelled extensively, I have found people receptive to the idea that Canada can play the role of host country in such an important experiment. The experiment is impor-
May 1, 1972

tant in so many ways, Mr. Speaker. I am thinking of the number of areas which have been touched on by those who have considered this question. It is important, surely, because it involves the question of arms proliferation and arms control. Today, the disarmament conference in Geneva is one where nations work diligently to bring about arms reduction. But, Mr. Speaker, what of an international disarmament strategy? What is our position there? What of a program that goes further than disarming the present arsenals and looks to the prevention of the buildup of further arsenals. These are the types of wide ranging and creative studies that a centre of this nature could pursue with a scholarly and impartial tone.
In addition to examining problems immediately relating to disarmament, which may be more political than we suspect, the university should also look at long term problems relating to disarmament. The experiment is also important in that it would examine questions of the environment that I referred to a moment ago. We could thereby prepare and formulate an international strategy for the solution or resolution of certain aspects of the international pollution problem. In addition, there is a series of related subject matters involving economics which needs to be considered in that context. Surely, these could be considered, since they involve such matters as the utilization of natural resources.
I suggest, also, that we could thereby consider the whole problem of international trade stability. The question of international trade stability has been of paramount importance to Canadians and their trading partners. We know only too well from our experience of the last eight months just how important that stability is. These problems become pretty significant in a crisis when we must deal with them on a short term basis and provide solutions that do little except meet in part the present, basic problem.
It is ironic that at present a United Nations conference on trade and development is being held in Santiago, Chile. We have sent a delegation to Chile; its mandate is not clear. There has been almost no discussion in this country of what we are to do to meet our responsibility to 80 per cent of the world's population which is struggling to find a role for itself. Increasingly, we have imported less from developing countries and more from developed countries. We seem to be moving away from a position that might offer real trading possibilities for developing countries of the world. Surely, the time has come for us to realize that we need more than short term, stopgap answers. We must plan better and deal with these questions more adequately. In my opinion, these studies could best be undertaken in a world university.
Even at the present we are considering seriously, or ought to be considering, what changes should be made in the charter of the United Nations, in order to make that charter more effective. There has been little discussion in this country about a review of the charter. All the same, that charter review is urgently needed.
When we talk about the world university, we are not talking about a typical, degree-granting institution. We are thinking more of a centre, or a series of centres, in which problems of vital importance for the existence and survival of mankind can be examined. It would not be, as U
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study Thant suggested, a university in the conventional sense. It would involve a flexible system enabling better co-operation among countries and the better integration of ideas and information. We need, as Mr. Ricketts suggested, a vehicle that will unite the world's academic resources; a vehicle which will complement our own work in this field. Canada's strategic and international position, which in some ways, may be said to be somewhat acute, makes the undertaking of this initiative, in my view, fundamentally important.
Let us examine the reasons as to why this is so. Considering the growing use of resources without plan or rationale throughout the world, Canada's own wealthy position in the world with regard to its own resources may become a source of real difficulty and hostility within the international community. I am thinking not only in terms of fuel resources, and minerals, but in terms of that resource which is perhaps most important to us all, water. We will need to maintain the stewardship of that water in some international context; otherwise, we may find ourselves in great jeopardy. Also, bearing in mind the continuing reliance of Canada on international trade, it is clear that every unresolved problem could be the source of some major trade crisis in future for this country. Canada's own commitment to arms control makes our involvement in the research and resolution of arms control strategies fundamental.
It is even important for us to concern ourselves with an international youth policy. I submit that since our population is basically youthful, our own involvement in international programs concerning youth will be a worth-while and necessary initiative.
So, in essence, Mr. Speaker, the establishment of this centre, of this world university, would be a major step in the resolution of many of our own fundamental problems.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH CENTRE TO CO-ORDINATE STUDIES OF WORLD PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) for introducing the notice of motion before the House and for giving the House an opportunity to debate this most important matter. Unfortunately, people have a tendency to forget the horrors of war when they are not immediately involved in or threatened by war. However, if we are to do something about war and maintain peace, we must act before we are on the threshold of conflict.
In his notice of motion the hon. member suggests that, to further United Nations' objectives, we should establish in Canada a world centre to administer and co-ordinate studies in three area, namely, (a) international relations and peace; (b) global problems of development; and, (c) the environment. Mr. Speaker, I did not interpret this notice of motion as recommending a world university, as suggested by the hon. member who introduced this notice of motion. According to my interpretation, the notice of motion recommends the establishment of an international research centre for peace, development, and the environment, and I will discuss it in that sense.
Since the notice of motion is divided into three sections, I will discuss it accordingly. May I say, first, that I fully support the proposal in part (a) of the motion. It is a sad fact that, in this country and throughout the world, we
1784

May 1, 1972
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study spend millions, even billions, of dollars on military research, and almost nothing on research related to peace. In Canada there is the Canadian Peace Research Institute, which attempts to study these questions; but that is a private body with a small budget and it receives very little government support. The Canadian Peace Research Institute was established in 1960, and was the first peace research institute established in the world. Actually, it was the first body to use the term, "peace research". At present, the Canadian Peace Research Institute has eight full-time employees in its office at Dundas, Ontario, and six in its Oakville office. Of these people, only eight are full-time researchers. The rest are office staff.
The chairman of the Canadian Peace Research Institute is Norman Alcock. He has been the main force behind it since its inception, although Alan and Hannah Newcombe have also been very prominent in its operations and have done a lot in the peace research area. At the present time, the only government help the Canadian Peace Research Institute receives is a grant from the Canada Council and a small grant from UNESCO. These are the only public grants it receives.
Some of the matters being studied by the Canadian Peace Research Institute are of the type I would like to see on a much broader basis by a government supported peace research institute, as seems to be suggested in part (a) of the hon. member's motion. Some of the projects that have been studied by the Canadian Peace Research Institute are studies on UN voting patterns and voting blocs, the prediction of war, attitudes on war-peace questions, the economic consequences of disarmament, peaceful nuclear explosions and disarmament, peace-keeping operations, and militarism, a survey on world trends. There are many others, but these are some of the studies being made by the institute in an attempt to understand the causes of conflict and the possible solutions to them.
There are other peace research institutes in the world, but they are very few. Some are privately financed and some are publicly financed. The most prominent one is in Sweden which, by the way, came about as a result of the influence of the privately sponsored Canadian institute. The Canadian institute came first. It prompted the establishment of the Swedish institute which is called the Swedish International Peace Research Institute. The government of Sweden gives the institute a grant of $1 million per year. The institute reports directly to parliament, but is not under the control of the government. It is free to study any matter it wishes relating to peace and war.
There is also an institute in Norway which is called the International Peace Research Institute of Oslo. This institute also receives government support, but not to the same extent as the one in Sweden. In Denmark, there is the Centre for Conflict Resolution which is also government supported. In West Germany, in the last fiscal year, the government provided $750,000 for peace research in universities.
In Holland there is the National Institute for study of Peace Questions. This institute receives a grant of $1 million per year for the government. The government of Holland also provides grants for peace research which

takes place in universities. There are other institutes of lesser importance.
The United States, which in many respects is one of the most powerful countries in the world, has no publicly financed peace research institute, although some research is going on in the universities. There is some research in the universities of Japan. On the whole, there is very little peace research being carried out in the world. It is interesting to note that with the commencement of the new university term next September, there will be a PhD course in peace research at Carleton University under the direction of John Sigler. This course should provide some interesting research and material, but it will be on a very small basis.
Let us compare this weak performance, not only in Canada but in the whole world, with research on military and related matters. In Canada, the government has provided in the estimates for 1972-73 a budget of $46 million under the title of defence research. There is another $5 million allocated for emergency measures. It seems strange that we provide $5 million for emergency measures, but hardly anything for peace research which might prevent those being used. If we look at the grants the Department of National Defence provides to private associations in Canada, we see they provide grants of $665,000. For such things as military studies at Canadian universities, they provide $280,000 and $70,000 in grants to rifle associations. There are grants to other types of cadet leagues and so on.
There may be real value in this type of funding by the federal government, but if we can allocate that much money to defence and military research, why can we not do a little more for peace research? According to the estimates, the Department of External Affairs gives major grants to three groups in Canada; $50,000 to the Canadian Institute of International Affairs; $27,000 to the UN Association in Canada and $2,500 to the Atlantic Council of Canada. These are good things, Mr. Speaker, but why can the government not give more money to a group such as the Canadian Peace Research Institute or for the establishment of a government peace research institute in Canada? The record of this government with regard to external aid is much better. I will discuss that later.
The government has already set up the Canadian International Development Research Centre which deals with the points in part (b) of the hon. member's motion. The amount of money allocated for that centre this year is $8 million. I will not deal with what is put forward in the hon. member's motion in that regard, because I think we already have that. If the governments of the world are sincere in their statements that their first priority is peace and their armies are only a means of security if aggression is committed, then surely they should spend a great deal more money on peace research and preventive measures. Governments should put their money where their talk is. If I were not in the House of Commons, I could put that much stronger.
At the present time, the behaviour of world governments is something like that of a man who spends a lot of money on fire insurance, but very little to prevent fires or like governments that spend a lot on medical treatment,
May 1, 1972

but little on preventative medicine. If we are sincerely concerned about peace in the world, we should know much more about the causes of war and the best means to reduce and eliminate these causes. Those persons who accept wars and world wars as inevitable and, consequently, state we can do nothing about them, are without imagination, foresight or courage. If their attitudes were to prevail, we would never conquer any pestilence, plague or evil. Fortunately, the spirit of man continually pushes forward and great cures and discoveries have been made.
One of the great disappointments of history is that while man has made great leaps forward in science, technology and medicine, there has not been much progress in human relationships, social dynamics, the reduction of violence and the reduction of war. Since 1945, the end of World War II, there have been 113 wars in the world, mostly in the third world. I can document those 113 wars if hon. members want me to do so.
I should like to refer to a document on this point. I have in my hand one of the bulletins put out by the Peace Research Institute which points out that in the 27 years since 1945 there have been 113 conflicts in the world. About half of these were of significant size, duration and intensity, there was slightly more than one every five months and any one of them was capable of provoking a holocaust. Some of these conflicts have been quite large. The tonnage of bombs dropped in the Korean war exceeded the tonnage dropped by all the allies in the Pacific theatre of World War II, and in Viet Nam the tonnage of bombs dropped has been greater than in all theatres of World War II. In addition, the Viet Nam war has lasted considerably longer than either World War I or World War II.
It is interesting to note that weapons deliveries to third world countries in recent years grew twice as fast as the gross national product of those countries. Many of us were shocked when we saw the budget figures for India and Pakistan at the time of the recent war which took place between them. These figures showed that in both countries the amount of money spent on defence and military equipment was more than 50 per cent of the budget.
I should also like to refer to another point made in this research extract. It is pointed out that the world now has a nuclear non-proliferation treaty which seeks to confine nuclear weapons to the big five nations. However, it points out that since 1945 all the killing in the wars I have referred to has been done by conventional weapons. In spite of this, the proliferation of conventional weapons, their spread from the few big countries which manufacture most of them to the many small countries who fight most of the wars, has continued unchecked and almost unnoticed.
Since the end of the war, the number of independent nations in the world has gone from 55 to 140. Only 13 of these manufacture armaments in any variety or quantity, yet 95 per cent of the conflicts since 1945 have been in the poorer countries. If the arms trade had not existed, those wars would either not have occurred or would have been fought with primitive weapons and therefore with much less destructiveness. My purpose in putting forward these
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study facts is to make this point as strongly as I can: if we are sincere in saying that we want to reduce world conflict, we should get off our butts and do something about it. Let us dedicate at least as much of our money to peace as we do to war.
What I have said so far related mainly to the first part of the hon. member's motion which suggests that we set up a world centre to co-ordinate and administer studies with respect to international relations and peace, and especially the problems of peace keeping, arms control and disarmament, human rights, and so on. With regard to part (b) of the motion, as I stated earlier the government has already taken action in this regard and has set up the International Development Research Centre. The budget for the centre provided by the government this year is $8 million. In addition to that, this year the government's budget for CIDA, the Canadian International Development Agency, is $483 million. I think that is significant. The government is doing a very good job regarding international development and I think international development has a lot to do with the reduction of world tension. However, that alone is not enough.
With respect to part (c) of the motion which deals with environmental problems, similarly I think the government has made considerable progress. It has set up the Department of the Environment. It has a research section and many studies are being conducted by the department. In addition, the Canadian government is taking a leadership role at the Stockholm conference. It is possible that the Stockholm conference will recommend that a more permanent structure be set up for dealing with world environment problems, and if that is the case I fully support such a proposal.
I do not think the government can be criticized in regard to sections (b) and (c) of the motion since it has made considerable effort in these areas. With regard to part (a), peace research, if we are serious and are not to be hypocritical about this, I think we must spend a lot more money in this area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to indicate my support for the motion put forward today by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald). Basically and essentially it says that we should support the establishment of a world university. Such a proposal is being considered by the United Nations. As the hon. member for Egmont said, to date Canada has not taken a position on the matter. This fact concerns me. If we do take a position and support it in principle, it does not mean necessarily that we will suddenly establish a university in Canada and then have to outline the details and technicalities of such a university. Rather, it is a question of giving support in principle. Apparently the only industrialized country that has indicated its support for the idea is Japan. Many other countries in the developing world support the idea as one in which they are interested.
This seems to me the type of motion that should receive the support of all parties in the House. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) has indicated his support, and I hope we will not see this resolution talked out as so many of them are. It is for this reason that I do not intend to speak at length and shall make only a few
25104-54J

May 1, 1972
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study points. I appeal to the government to allow us, before the hour is up, to pass the motion and I ask that the government, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), take a definite stand on the question and support it in principle.
The hon. member for Egmont outlined a number of matters that a world university would have to deal with, such as international relations, peace keeping, nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation of arms, and so on. Then he talked about the problem of development in the third world. We are also concerned about environmental problems and problems of science and technology. We in Canada have a great deal at stake in this regard. We must first of all realize that we are a global village, that what happens on the other side of the world has a great impact upon us in Canada. We must interest ourselves in the other peoples of the world and create a better understanding of their feelings, wishes and aspirations. We cannot go back to the old days when each country was isolated from others, formed its own policies and simply hoped for the best.
In light of today's world, international politics and the use of weaponry, national boundaries no longer exist. Neither do they exist in the field of pollution, science and technology. We must accept the fact that the institutions of man are lagging far behind. This is one of the many reasons that so many people in the world feel upset and restless at the type of institutions which man creates.
Another point I must make is that in debates such as this we always hear wonderful speeches containing platitudes about people and what they want do do, but action never seems to be taken. Hon. members on all sides suggest solutions for understanding one another better, yet out of the other side of their mouth they continue talking about the same old policies. For example, in the United States the President is talking of international co-operation, about how the big powers must begin to understand one another. At the same time, he is ordering bombing attacks on North Viet Nam. This type of hypocrisy in the world must cease. Hopefully, a world university would make a contribution toward ending this kind of hypocritical attitude on the part of some of the big powers.
War is big business. We spend billions of dollars every year on scientific research and development of armaments. Countries on each side of the world are trying to develop more sophisticated ways of killing, maiming and injuring others; they are developing more sophisticated napalm bombs to drop on women and children in various parts of the world. There is this tremendous emphasis in our society, yet we do very little to foster peace or international development.
We in Canada could do a great deal in that direction if we really wanted to. We have the defence production agreement with the United States. Certain products under that agreement go the United States military complex and find their way into Viet Nam. In that way our country is indirectly involved in the war in Viet Nam. We should not be a party to such things; we should be spending the money going into that agreement on peace research,

research into international pollution and environmental problems, promoting world trade, and so on.
We in Canada belong to NORAD. We spend a great deal of money every year on NORAD, but where does it get us? Even some military experts in the United States say NORAD is obsolete and nothing but a waste of money. Why do we not terminate that arrangement and immediately divert the money into projects such as a world university and international development?
We participate in NATO. I question the usefulness of NATO. I say Canada should get out of NATO and concentrate more on international organizations such as the United Nations. I want to make it very clear that this is the direction in which I want Canada to go. Unless we do some of these things, all the speeches we make in this chamber are useless. We talk like nice guys but continue putting money into weaponry to continue the bombing of people in Viet Nam. Unless Canada takes action and gets out of NORAD and NATO by terminating the defence sharing agreements, all our words will be meaningless.
We also carry out research at Suffield, Alberta, in chemical and biological warfare. What is the purpose of this but to develop more sophisticated ways of killing people? This type of research should be terminated. If we really want to put our muscle where our words and our mouths are, we should be doing the things I have mentioned. I know that to many members of the House this may sound like a radical and irresponsible way to go. I do not think it is. I think Canada as a middle power must take a stand such as this. We are a respected nation throughout the world and could provide a great deal more leadership than we are now.
We had an example of our leadership in the recognition of the People's Republic of China. I think we made a contribution there. But that is only a small step in the direction of things we could be doing if Canada became more aggressive and independent in foreign affairs policy, doing something real for the international community.
There are other matters I could mention about a world university and why we should move in that direction. We in Canada, besides considering world problems have a number of parochial matters at stake. Canada has resources that we and other countries want and may need. What will our long-term policy be respecting non-renewable resources? These are questions that could be studied at a world university.
The resource of water was mentioned earlier in this debate. We must consider the question of international trade now that Great Britain and three other countries are joining the European Common Market. We now have Europe, the United States, the eastern and Japanese blocs. Where does Canada fit into this type of trade complex? And what is our future? These are a few of the parochial questions in which Canada is tremendously interested and which could be studied by a world university. For these reasons I support the motion before us.
In a few words I should like to caution some hon. members about one or two situations that may develop if we are not careful. We have a number of institutions around the world studying topics such as I have men-
May 1, 1972

tioned, including peace keeping, disarmament, etc. The results of many of these studies have had little impact upon the powers that be; they seem to be very aloof. If we do establish a world university we will have to make it our purpose that such a world centre has real impact on the powers that be: it must have relevance to the powers that be, and links with the decision-making people in world society. Such a university should have relevance to and impact upon the peoples of all countries of the world.
Too often under our foreign aid and international development programs we do not consult the people in the developing countries. We consult only the leaders of these people and we make decisions according to the benefits that may accrue to some multinational corporation or to the departments of external affairs and trade and commerce. We tend to ignore the little guy of the third world. It is this person whom we must not ignore; it is this person whom we must consult and help.
With that in mind, I certainly support this motion and our party supports it. This is a worth-while project to put our money into. I appeal to the cabinet and government backbenchers not to talk it out, but to help us on this side, and members such as the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, pressure our Secretary of State for External Affairs into taking a decisive stand for once, putting the muscle of Canada into an approach that is worth while and which, I am quite sure, will count in a real way on the world scene.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), so far as I am able to understand it, seems to be directed toward the establishment of a centre which would draw together but duplicate the work being done in committees and institutions of the UN and other international bodies. Each of the three great issues-we do not deny for one moment that they are great issues-is the subject of continual examination. It would seem by his motion that the hon. member wants to have all these activities come together into one centre to be established in Canada.
While the co-ordination and co-operation among the many bodies now existing could undoubtedly be improved so that the ultimate results of their studies and deliberations would be more fruitful, I suggest that yet another body is not necessarily the way to do this. It would result in more duplication of the work of others already in the field, and for a long time would not even do that very well.
The hon. member's motion specifies three great issues which are worthy of further research and co-ordination. However, it seems to me that basically the motion is calling for research into what can provide the political, economic and social elements of the peace which the vast majority of the world's people desire. This basic question, probably the greatest, is also the subject of study and research in many countries, Canada included. The UN General Assembly recognized the need for co-ordination in this field in December, 1971, when it passed, by a large majority, resolution 2817. That resolution notes the work done in the field of peace research by national and international institutions, by the UN educational, scientific and
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study
cultural organization and the UN institute for training and research.
The United Nation's Secretary General is instructed by the resolution to prepare biennially, and he has already begun to do so, an informative report on scientific works produced by national, international, governmental and non-governmental, public and private institutions in the field of peace research. Therefore, with the co-operation of Canada, since our delegation co-sponsored this resolution, some of the very basic work which the hon. member would have his world centre undertake has already commenced at our existing world centre, the United Nations. I suggest our efforts should concentrate on making more effective the machinery we have already, machinery into which is built an immense amount of experience and expertise, rather than start all over again.
The fact that these three great global issues still defy solution is due not to lack of knowledge and the exchange of information but, rather, to the competing policies and philosophies of the world's states. A Canadian government-financed research centre, however well organized and staffed could-

I think I can say it without reading it for your benefit. Such a centre could not very well eliminate all this rivalry. The rival powers could still preclude the possibility of translating the studies of the centre into effective action. It has been said that the United Nations is an accurate reflection of an imperfect world. It is that imperfect world which hinders the furtherance of the objectives of the United Nations. That imperfect world, not the lack of studies and co-ordination, also delays significant action to alleviate the hon. member's three issues of international relations and peace, global problems of development and the impact of science and technology on the environment.
Few subjects can have come under such a degree of interdisciplinary and international scrutiny and discussion as disarmament and arms control. Individually and collectively, scientists, scholars, statesmen and soldiers have grappled with the problem of reducing armaments while maintaining international security. The problem has been one of main concern at the United Nations and in various special negotiating bodies, in particular the disarmament conference in Geneva in which Canada participates. While no one can deny that these discussions include their share of empty verbiage, they also stimulate ideas, assessments and proposals based on substantial international thought and research.
Last year, for instance, the United Nations produced a major report on the economic and social consequences of the arms race. This report was prepared by a group of scientists and scholars from western, Soviet and non-aligned countries, including a distinguished Canadian professor. A Canadian was also a member of a similar team which drew up a United Nations' report on chemical and biological warfare in 1969.
A glance through the annual report of the disarmament conference in Geneva shows that this body's work, though

May 1, 1972
Suggested Centre for World Problems Study
essentially political, also benefits from solid technical study and analysis. Some of the topics dealt with in recent background working papers include many things, such as employment of ocean-bottom seismographs to improve present detection capability for seismic events and possibly to increase the capability of identifying explosions from natural events as well, aspects of the definition of toxins and a method to determine, in numerical terms, the usefulness of particular seismic discriminations to the political decision problems posed by nuclear test ban control with or without obligatory inspections.
Canada has contributed fully to the technical background of the Geneva discussions. For instance, in 1971 the Canadian delegation submitted papers on atmospheric sensing and verification of a ban on development, production and stockpiling of chemical weapons, and seismo-logical detection and identification of underground nuclear explosion.
In Canada, studies and analyses of arms and disarmament problems are carried on in the normal course of their work by officials of the departments of external affairs and national defence. They are able to keep in touch with thinking in other countries through the usual diplomatic channels and through international conferences, particularly the disarmament committee in Geneva. Moreover, Canadian universities are devoting increasing attention to arms control and disarmament as part of their international relations or strategic studies programs, and are being encouraged in doing so by federal government grants.
Specialists in these fields from the academic world and the public service are continually exchanging views and ideas both through informal contact at home and abroad and at more formal gatherings such as the seminars organized from time to time by the Canadian Institute of International Affairs. This institute has in recent years made a major effort to stimulate research and publication in this general field, and other private organizations take a serious interest in the question of disarmament.
In short, in the field of disarmament there is no lack of interest or activity by highly qualified people who remain well aware of each other's work though their activities are not always co-ordinated through a formal structure. They are making an invaluable, indeed essential contribution toward the eventual slowing down and termination of the arms race. The slowness of progress in this field is not the result of anybody's failure or inability to keep informed but, rather, of an insufficient will on the part of a number of world states to seek resolution of their differences by peaceful means.
I would also like to speak on another matter pertaining to the hon. member's motion. The motion provides an opportunity to focus on a great task which confronts Canada and the other developed and developing nations of the world. Acknowledgement of one part of this problem of importance to all Canadians formed the climax of President Nixon's recent visit. I would bring to the attention of the hon. member that the signing of the Great Lakes water control agreement to begin to restore the Great Lakes did not have to await the formation of a new research and co-ordination centre. Drawing on the studies and recommendations of the International Joint Commission and other bodies, procedures for effective action have been formulated.
The Great Lakes problem is a complicated and expensive one to solve. The impact of science and technology, especially the deleterious effects which these advances have had on environment throughout the world, also will be complicated and expensive to solve. The handling of the relatively local situation in the Great Lakes is compounded by the authorities of several jurisdictions. It is not difficult to project this to the national, hemispheric or global stage to realize that here is a world wide matter which requires maximum co-ordination and co-operation so that the complementary and competing needs and desires of the world's peoples can be met to the maximum degree possible. The achievement of this requires, also, utilization of a vast wealth of data, special studies, highly professional skills and so on.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before private members' hour I had an opportunity to pay my respectful tribute to the work in the field of penal reform of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I would also like to recall to the House the contributions made by other hon. members, most notably the late Don Brown, the former member for Essex West. That hon. member, with Senator Hayden, was joint chairman of the Senate and House of Commons committee which considered this subject in the 1950s.
A former prime minister, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon indicated how difficult it is to discuss rationally the question of crime and punishment. He made it perfectly clear that

May 1, 1972

those who oppose corporal punishment do not do so out of any false sentiment. The hon. member for Prince Albert and others who oppose the imposition of corporal punishment do so for the simple reason that this form of punishment has not and will not do any good.
Many people in our society linger under the impression that what is important in restraining and deterring crime is the severity of punishment, but we know from history that this is not so. The records of the nineteenth century tell us of little children having been hanged for theft, of men and women having been brutally whipped for committing very small offences. In general, the early part of the nineteenth century was characterized both in Europe and in North America by great violence, and these severe punishments, far from deterring the commission of crime perhaps escalated it.
Over many years society has found out that the real deterrent to crime has been the certainty of apprehension and of conviction at trial. This is a lesson which it is difficult for many people to accept, because it is much easier to believe that there is a quick and simple solution to crime, that we have it within our power to do something which is relatively easy and inexpensive in order to prevent the commission of crime. But in fact, as every member of the House knows, the control of crime in modern society will cost money and the devotion of a great deal of governmental effort.
To control crime we need better policemen, more respect for police forces, better rapport between the police and the public, an attack on some of the basic social causes of crime, better courts, more facilities, more judges and-I hesitate to say it-perhaps even more lawyers. The whole process of trial should not be so drawn out and subject to all kinds of unusual accidents and hazards. The total process should be carried on rationally in the interests of defending society and also of protecting the rights of those charged. I can recall that when the report of the committee was prepared in 1956, a senior senator on the committee remarked to me that it marked "the end of an illusion", the illusion that there is an easy way out, a simple way of dealing with serious crime.
I should like to make one or two comments on the merits of the longstanding discussion on corporal punishment in this country. I commend, for the consideration of hon. members, the report of the joint Senate and House of Commons committee representing, as I said earlier, three years of work during the course of which the committee heard expert evidence on the subject not only from Canada but from Great Britain, the United States and elsewhere. I think at that time the committee's investigation constituted something of a novelty in our parliament and still stands as a great accomplishment in terms of parliamentary inquiry.
One thing the committee noted immediately was that corporal punishment had become a very rare event; it was applied only in a minute percentage of the cases where it could have been applied. In much less than 1 per cent of the cases where corporal punishment could have been imposed was it actually applied in the middle 1950s, and we know that its use as a punishment since that time has
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 become increasingly rarer. We might ask ourselves why this should be. In asking that question we are faced with the formidable answer that the collective judgment of those who are most concerned with the administration of justice, be they police, courts, penal officials, in fact experts of every kind, is that it is a useless punishment. This is why corporal punishment is rare. Its imposition has not been reduced because of any sentimental impulse on the part of people charged with the administration of justice, but simply because long experience has taught them that it has done no good.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said in this House last Friday that the retention of corporal punishment was necessary to deter the commission of violent crime. He thereby committed the illogical indiscretion of failing to explain why violent crime had occurred even when this type of punishment remained in the Criminal Code. It is a punishment that has almost grown out of date because of the judgment of people that it is useless. In 1956, the committee noted that in most countries corporal punishment had been abandoned and that before it had been abandoned it had ceased to be used. The committee commented as follows:
In this respect, Canada would appear to be in line with other democratic countries which abandoned corporal punishment after its use had steadily decreased over a considerable period of time.
Another feature of the discussion on corporal punishment is the suggestion that it might have special utility for young offenders. This suggestion was made last Friday by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and it has been repeated on many occasions in the course of discussions on this subject. It has been suggested that a quick spanking or caring would have more effect on a young offender than his being put in prison or being subjected to other types of treatment. The committee anticipated the argument of the hon. member for Oxford because at one stage its report states:
Several witnesses suggested corporal punishment might be particularly effective against this type of offender-
They had been speaking about leather-jacketed hooligans.
-because it would humiliate him in the eyes of his companions and take away the false glamour attached to a person who had been unaffected by lesser punishments.
However, the committee then noted the reservation which was expressed even by those who advocated this course of action. I quote again from the report at page 44, where people advocating this kind of treatment for young offenders stated:
Some form of pre-sentence investigation and report was suggested which would take into account physical, mental, emotional, environmental, and other relevant factors in the background of the offender. This was considered to be necessary, particularly in the case of young offenders who had not proven amenable to other methods of correction and who might be so constituted as to suffer grave harm from the infliction of corporal punishment.
Wherever the committee pursued the arguments for the retention of corporal punishment it came to the conclusion, after serious investigation of the available evidence and the opinions of experts from all over the world, that those arguments would not bear up. Perhaps it would be most helpful if I were to quote one of its general conclusions. This passage is taken from page 45 of the report:

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
Generally, in relation to all types of offenders, those favouring abolition argue that corporal punishment could produce no quick cure and was apt to do positive harm. The rarity of the sentence in Canada meant that its imposition was inconsistent and inequitable, a factor recognized by representatives of the police. Its imposition, under present conditions, depended upon the views of particular judges and, perhaps, also the swings of public opinion; and sometimes bore little relation to the nature of offences or offenders. It was considered a degrading punishment; and, since it was more likely to arouse feelings of resentment and revenge, it was urged that public humiliation of offenders could not be a proper foundation for their reform. To bring out the best in young offenders, better methods of treatment could be employed and, to protect society from recidivists and sexual offenders, isolation and segregation could be used to greater effect. Although no specific evidence was produced, the opinion was expressed that corporal punishment might adversely affect prison officials either by bringing out sadistic impulses or discouraging the application of positive reformative measures.
Thereafter, the committee considered in detail the pointed question as to whether or not corporal punishment deterred the commission of further offences by persons to whom it was applied. At one stage in the committee's investigation, on its behalf I personally investigated the cases of approximately 20 people who had been subjected to corporal punishment. I interviewed them all. My distinct recollection of this experience was that corporal punishment could not be said to have done the least bit of good for any of those men. In fact, I could well remember, many years after the event, that in describing what had happened to them their eyes blazed and the hair on the back of their neck raised. I remembered how bitter they became.
I accept entirely the view of the committee that corporal punishment, far from deterring the commission of further crimes by people to whom it is applied, is much more likely to create a situation in their minds which will make reform more difficult and a continuing criminal career more likely. The committee also considered in great detail whether there was any evidence that the presence or absence of corporal punishment in general had any effect in restraining the commission of crime. Although the view of many people may be that severe punishment such as corporal punishment might have this effect, certainly it does not stand up under investigation and the committee concluded that corporal punishment does not exercise any unique deterrent effect in addition to that provided by other methods of punishment.
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in going through the committee's report is to indicate that this matter has been seriously considered by parliament, and that a very superior parliamentary committee representing both Houses many years ago found that corporal punishment as a judicial sentence did no good and recommended its abolition. I think that if we accept the recommendations contained in the bill before us, and abolish corporal punishment, we will accomplish a great legal reform.
I should like to mention that there is a difference between the recommendations of the committee of which I have been speaking and the bill. The committee recommended the abolition of corporal punishment as a judicial sentence, but it did not recommend its abolition as a punishment in our penal institutions. The reason was that at that time the Commissioner of Penitentiaries and his [DOT]

staff considered it necessary to retain this form of punishment as an ultimate sanction in the preserving of discipline in penitentiaries. The committee, although accepting that view, was of the opinion that it should be used only rarely, in special circumstances and under conditions of complete control. The committee recommended, for example, that it should not be used except with the express permission of the Commissioner of Penitentiaries.
The result has been that over the years the use of corporal punishment as a method of discipline in our penitentiaries has decreased. As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) pointed out in his address last Friday, the former commissioner of penitentiaries, when giving evidence to the justice committee a year or two ago, expressed the view that it was no longer necessary as a disciplinary sanction in penitentiaries. Therefore, the recommendation contained in this bill, that corporal punishment be abolished both in the judicial sense and as a form of punishment in our penitentiaries, seems to be supported by the evidence and the experience both in the courts and in the penal system.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of this address I said that society is concerned with the rise in crimes of violence and violence in general. Not unnaturally, people in society seek to find quick solutions to these problems; they seek easy answers for violence and crime. But I suggest that there are no easy answers. Certainly, the least effective of the answers suggested is that of severe punishment, such as corporal punishment, because it has no good effect. We do ourselves credit in facing up to this reality, and perhaps we can lead the people of this country to a better understanding of the fundamentals of our society. If we are to have less crime and less violence, the social causes of crime must be attacked and, as a country, we must be prepared to spend far more money and devote much better people to the control of crime in our police forces, in our judicial systems and in our treatment systems.
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken of only one aspect of this bill but I have listened with great interests to the comments of hon. members on all the other subjects, including aerial hijacking about which I have had deep concern. I hope that this bill will shortly be referred to the committee so that it can be considered in detail, brought back to the House and enacted into law.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is now dealing with Bill C-2, to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to the Criminal Code 1967 Amendment Act, the Criminal Records Act, the National Defence Act, the Parole Act and the Visiting Forces Act.
Mr. Speaker, no human need is more essential than that of individual security, no desire more instinctive than that of being free from fear. If one does not feel secure at home or in the street, if one is threatened-by an agent of a police state or by a criminal or even by discriminatory economic forces-one is not safe any more. In that sense, the legendary freedom of the Canadian people is eroded more and more every day.
May 1, 1972

Social disorders, bludgeon laws, undue union thrusts, violence, increased discrimination, the frustration felt by more and more citizens in the presence of the enormous wealth of this country, such are the characteristics of a situation that is painful to describe when one knows that our ancestors always stood with such conviction for freedom.
In the face of those modern problems, to provide protection which is the basis of freedom and security is the first duty of a government in the judicial field. Now, today, more and more people question the judicial power. To quote but one example, I say that the too great influence of party politics and money in the administration of justice have been the cause of a greater and greater lack of confidence of the people in the judicial power, which is something very serious.
The appointment of judges is often a matter of politics. The same can be said of the bail system, which often enables the rich to come off well and causes the poor to rot behind the slow administrative process of justice.
Finally, to be free as well as secure, one must have some financial security, which, unfortunately, is the case of fewer and fewer Canadians.
This explains the feelings of frustration, of dissent, of violence, which are not only modern social phenomena, but mostly the result of a provoking economic policy which leads us to obvious social injustice. That is why we must strive after a policy of fair distribution and try to eliminate those understandable feelings of frustration.
Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal to say about the whole concept of justice. Let us say right away that an incomplete and partial revision of the Criminal Code, as proposed in the bill before us, does not necessarily mean a reform of justice. We shall have to consider it at length and go much further.
By the way, does the minister know where we are heading with this minor reform? The criminal law must be a changing and evolutive tool of social order, and I am disappointed when I realize that instead of going all out in that direction, that goal, the government is satisfied with minor reforms, except for clause 24, which abolishes the additional punishment of whipping.
This is a very good measure which comes, once again, too late.
Bill C-2 is a kind of omnibus bill, dealing with several matters, such as the breathalyzer false alarms, conditional discharges, and so on.
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to deal with some of these points and make a constructive criticism.
Insofar as conditional discharges are concerned, I shall refer to new clauses 545 and 662.1 of the bill. In short, the government proposes to broaden, once more, the Parole Act, in order to make it more flexible and workable.
The concept of the public interest is also invoked in those two sections and it is stated that parole will be granted in cases other than those previously provided for where the interests of the accused are not contrary to those of the public.
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
That is a new concept in this act on parole, but no definition of public interest is given, which can lead us to asking ourselves questions.
In this connection, I shall bring up a point at this time. On the one hand, the government broadens the act on parole to include other categories of accused while, on the other hand, the same government does not set up any mechanism for the control, the probation or the rehabilitation of the accused discharged either conditionally or unconditionally.
Mr. Speaker, I have statistics on this in my office, but off-hand one can surely say that every parole officer must deal with at least 20 to 30 criminals. Surely then he cannot deal with each prisoner to whom parole is granted, either conditionally or unconditionally, on an individual, human and personalized basis.
And so, Mr. Speaker, we read the type of news recently published in the Gazette to the effect that the crime rate is increasing in Canada, that experience with parole is more or less satisfactory, more often than not, unfortunate, and that a system of control, of review, should be adopted in that field.
Who makes up that Parole Board? Competent people, people who are interested in that field? It does not comprise more than ten members who simply travel across Canada, through areas they know more or less, and who often make decisions that are contrary to that of the judge, so that in many cases the work accomplished by the Parole Board renders that of the judge useless. And so the lack of planning and co-ordination becomes evident.
Mr. Speaker, if the government wants to broaden the law on parole, it will have to set up, in due course, a control or probation mechanism for each prisoner, to allow for his case being followed.
I have personally visited some prisons and the Social Welfare Court in Montreal. I have met some judges, I have talked with them and I have attended hearings. What I have seen is absolutely incredible, indeed it is an indescribable chaos. There are some people who are endeavouring to administer justice as best they can in spite of the bureaucracy, inadequate legislation and the lack of a rehabilitation system, as a result of which the same judge constantly sees the same individuals from one generation to another. This shows, Mr. Speaker, how our crime prevention system is inadequate.
To give you another quite typical example, I have always wondered why the parole legislation could not apply to young delinquents. For a criminal who has been condemned eight or ten times, I have data published in Hansard in reply to a question of mine to the Minister of Justice. After being condemned more than 20 times, some criminals re-apply for parole and the Board grants their request. They are hardened criminals; I should say professional criminals.
However, a young delinquent, after his first or second offence, is not eligible for parole. Nevertheless, if there is someone who would have some chance of being rehabilitated, of straightening up, of becoming respectful of social order, it is that young man. But instead of that, he is jailed with other young people, sometimes even with hardened

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 criminals and when he is freed, he is at least twice as bad as before,
Mr. Speaker, those prisons or detention centres are practically crime schools and it is sad to note that no immediate or realistic step is taken.
Parole is granted to a hardened, professional criminal, while a young first offender will rot in a detention centre with homosexuals, criminals guilty of assault and battery, burglary, attempted rape, etc. When he is freed, this youngster is briefed about ways to commit crimes. He has been living in this. No one cared to rehabilitate him in a very personal way. Finally, we make a criminal out of him.
I will remind the House of an unfortunate incident which took place in Hull. A criminal, whose name I cannot remember, killed a policeman sometime ago, in the city of Hull. This same criminal had been taken under probation by the brother of the policeman who was killed. This indicates how difficult it is to rehabilitate a hardened criminal, even when he is given very special and personal care.
So, what do we do with our young offenders? If it is so hard with hardened criminals, what are we waiting for to help these youngsters who, very often, appear before the Welfare court judge, precisely because they have not lived in a good family circle, because their parents lacked money, or for any other kinds of reasons? What do we do? Absolutely nothing. Petty reforms with a lot of publicity, and that is all!
It seems that we lack logic. If we are truly concerned with justice in Canada, we must tackle this problem without delay.
Mr. Speaker, even if we have fair laws, the best judges, the best judicial system in the world, if the people who enforce the law-I mean the police forces, among others- do not enjoy the confidence of the authorities and are put, by the political power, in positions such that they can give even give rise to violence, in short, if morale among our police forces is low, it is useless to think that justice will be improved in Canada, no matter what legislation is introduced.
And that relates to the problem of capital punishment.
A few years ago, in Victoriaville, officer Collard was called to the scene of a crime with another policeman in order to arrest the perpetrators of a burglary. Not only did the bandits escape but they fired at the policemen. In fact, officer Collard lost 12 months of work, because of the wounds received on that occasion. The bandit was jailed, he applied for parole and our very intelligent and very brilliant Parole Board granted the parole without imposing any control nor appointing any probation officer. The same man, a little later, commits another burglary in Sainte-Therese-de-Blainville and kills another policeman.
Then, policemen will be told, enforce the law, get closer to the people, go out and risk your life.
Mr. Speaker, on the one hand, our police forces are asked to risk their lives for the welfare of society, while at the same time nothing is done to administer justice prop-

erly. What is the use of chasing a criminal if, once he is arrested, he is immediately released without probation or control? What is the use of police forces if justice is not administered logically, in spite of the amounts spent to track down criminals?
Mr. Speaker, I believe that that is a basic problem.
A policeman in Drummondville, in the riding of the Minister of Industry, Trade, and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who is not here at present, is crippled for life; he uses a wheelchair and he cannot work. Why? Because he went to the scene of a crime, tried to arrest the criminal and was fired upon. The criminal was caught a little later and released under the rules governing the famous Parole Board.

speechtext:
Why should this or that police officer or police corps be required to show concern, courage and good will in their work when justice is not administered efficiently.
This does not necessarily mean that capital punishment should be requested in all cases involving criminal law. It means that the time has come for the administration of justice to be logical. If it is worth while to allot money to the tracking down of criminals and to their rehabilitation, to the application of laws, to the maintenance of police services which are becoming more and more expensive to operate, it is certainly worth while to tackle this problem and follow up on the convicts afterwards. Every possible means to rehabilitate them should be taken, if the majority wishes so. But at least let us take these steps rather than fail in our task as happened with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) with respect to the National Parole Board. The Solicitor General, I suggest, acts something like a clown. When during one week-end he releases prisoners who all do return to jail, he says: My program is an excellent one. During the following week-end, some of those he has released fail to come back and then he says: The Board's program is not that good; they are to be blamed. When results are good, he gets the credit; when they are not, he blames the Board. But whatever the outcome, the Solicitor General is never available. He is satisfied with the publicity made around his successful week-ends. When there is failure, he sinks his head in the sand like an ostrich and dares not face the problem.
Mr. Speaker, it follows that the population is asking questions about the administration of justice. In fact, people want politics to be divorced from the administration of justice in Canada. Canadians would like to see some measure of responsibility in the enforcement of laws and some respect for the Criminal Code.
