Mr. Speaker, I don't have these figures on hand, and rather than quote a figure of which I am not sure, I prefer to send this information to the hon. member who is asking the question. If he is genuinely interested, I shall send him the documents that the Solicitor General distributes to all members. However, the statistics are there to prove the point.
There is no doubt that in the case of some criminal offenders, it is worthwhile to try everything to rehabilitate them. I would even be inclined to believe, Mr. Speaker, that in most cases, since they are human beings who may have made one, two or three mistakes in their lifetime, we have the duty to respect not only the law but also the individuals. But, this means also that the government is not afraid of assuming their responsibilities and taking all available means to protect society.
Actually, the background of all those problems is the same. When you go to the Welfare Court-and I invite my colleagues to do so-and meet young delinquents, you realize that most of them are there precisely because the family environment was either totally lacking-they are children who grew up in the streets-or rotten to the core. When the family, for financial, marital or other reasons cannot assume its responsibilities toward a child, more often than not he will become a delinquent.
Furthermore, the system of rehabilitation of young delinquents is inadequate and practically inexistant, first because of a shortage of probation officers and second because the Parole Act cannot be applied to these young people. For several similar reasons, the centre eventually becomes a school of crime.
When the family and society have failed to rehabilitate a young delinquent, should we convict him, when we all share the guilt for that situation?
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the problem of young delinquents is now the most urgent in the field of administration of justice in Canada and that it is inacceptable that today nothing is being done about it. Even the co-operation which should take place between provincial and federal governments has become inexistent.
I should like to say something else about the bill: there is to be in the near future a review of the abolition of capital punishment.
The hon. Minister of Justice has promised repeatedly that a debate would be held in the House on this issue, giving all hon. members an opportunity to speak for or against capital punishment. Mr. Speaker, I personally carried out a survey in my riding. I sent out 17,885 copies of a questionnaire to families, asking them: "Are you for or against, give me your opinion."
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
Frankly, the response from those people was extraordinary. Indeed I should appreciate our having an opportunity in this House to tell the government what the people of Lotbiniere think of this issue, of social order and justice in general. For that, Mr. Speaker, the minister will have to stop promising a debate on capital punishment and grant it. Let the government stop putting it off indefinitely and give hon. members an opportunity to express the views of their constituents in this House.
All my colleagues have made similar inquiries and, needless to say, Mr. Speaker, opinions differ. How can it be otherwise? But precisely because this is a very important subject on which opinions differ, we must hold this debate in the House of Commons and deal with this issue immediately.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude my remarks by stating that it is an undeniable fact recognized by all members that criminality or the crime rate in Canada is increasing.
There is a second thing that must be said: the cost of the administration of justice in Canada is soaring.
There is a third thing that must also be said: movements of violence, frustration, dissent are increasingly serious in Canada, are also increasing.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, the crime rate among the young is rising alarmingly and distressingly.
These are four facts that, if related, point to a common source, a common problem. When you ask the government to establish more intelligent and more adequate rehabilitation systems, when you ask it to provide more adequate structures and equipment for the administration of justice, the government replies that it lacks money.
Actually, if rehabilitation is not more advanced in Canada, Mr. Speaker, it is because we have no money. If there are so many criminals in Canada, it is simply because wealth and poverty live side by side, and that such flagrant injustice causes people to revolt, commit crimes, and so on and so forth-
This past week-end, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson) announced that members of the Canadian Armed Forces would be instructed in riot prevention and control methods. This, Mr. Speaker, is another problem of modern times. All of this results from the fact that there exists in Canada-we shall have to recognize this one of these days-a basic economic problem; it is not because our Bill of Rights and all our other legislation say that "all Canadians are equal", or that it is written in our Criminal code that "all citizens are equal and will be treated as equals before the law" that we must believe that they actually are. For they are not, Mr. Speaker, and to believe otherwise is to delude oneself!
We all know that poverty and unemployment prevail in all parts of Canada. We all know that many families who depend on social welfare hand-outs cannot make ends meet with their meager monthly allowances.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, if the Canadian family- the basic unit of our society-is deprived of the necessary financial means of survival, it will continue to break up more and more as it has done over the past 10 years,

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 which will unavoidably result in an increased criminal index, in spite of the considerable amounts of money we may invest in the rehabilitation of criminals and the administration of justice.
Mr. Speaker, this reminds me of some sort of poultice on a wooden leg. Instead of dealing with the problems which generate criminals who, because of their utmost poverty and destitution, are induced into stealing, rebelling and joining protest or violence groups, the government will rather tackle the sequels of the problems such as the rise in the crime rate. Then, what do they do to reduce this rate? Criminals are let out on bail and without being rehabilitated so much so that poverty and frustration continue to increase in our society. In final analysis, the crime rate is rising and those criminals freed on bail continue to be criminals.
I wish to refer my colleagues to answers given by the former Minister of Justice to questions which I had put on the Order Paper and they will then realize as I said before, how this can be so ridiculous.
Criminals of the type we find in Kingston's penitentiary, Mr. Speaker, have been convicted more than 20 times and have been paroled after their twenty-first conviction.
In other words, the Parole Board is sheer window-dressing on the part of the government which hopes to conceal his inability to correct the situation concerning the administration of justice. It is more or less a means of politely getting rid of criminals while keeping a good front under the prextext of respecting the human being.
There being no probation and control methods, criminals are left to fend for themselves. It follows that the crime rate goes on increasing in Canada and the situation keeps on worsening.
Mr. Speaker, in short now is the time to keep politics out of justice and to have all citizens treated equally before the law. The bail system should be entirely revamped, as I said at the beginning of my remarks. Imprisonment does not last very long for the well-to-do and they finally get away with it. However, the penniless must wait because of the slowness of the administrative process because they have no money to put up for bail.
In the field of justice, money is becoming an important factor. If it is true that all Canadians are equal and can enjoy freedom and security, the government should start by setting up some sensible and modern financial machinery to meet the probems of a modern society through distributive justice.
Secondly, the government should set up at all costs a rehabilitation and probation system for all criminals likely to be rehabilitated.
Last but not least, the government should take steps as soon as possible to rehabilitate juvenile delinquents who are perhaps the most neglected and who most need our attention.
In fact, those people cannot make themselves heard and it is our duty as members of Parliament to defend them.
I urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) to look into this problem and to take the steps required to put some order in this system.

In conclusion, I would point out that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Ouellet) made not only an offensive but a dishonest remark about Creditiste members.
The same member over the last three years, has risen in his seat exactly 14 times, and he now takes the liberty of making derogatory and dishonest remarks about his colleagues. I think that if his constituents knew that over a period of three years, even as parliamentary secretary, he spoke only 14 times, while the Creditiste members spoke on average more than twice a day, they would realize that government members are more interested in indulging in petty politics than in actually governing the country.
Once again tonight, he is conspicuous by his absence as usual. That is why he did not manage to speak more than 14 times in three years.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be approriate to deal at length with the bill now before us.
As a member of the legal profession and of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, I simply want to state a few general principles which seem to underlie this legislation.
The bill before us purports to strike a balance between the maintenance of order and the fair treatment to be meted out to offenders. We should avoid a treatment that is imbued with a spirit of revenge. It should instead be characterized by the wish to rehabilitate the accused. Still, that balance is difficult to achieve, since the principles involved are to my mind of equal importance.
I must admit that this bill arouses both fear and hope in me.
It arouses fear because it seems to grant exceptional importance to those who break the law, or who are willing to do so. Of course, I do not claim that those who have made one or two errors are not entitled to some compassion and justice. But I have noticed that often the funds spent on their rehabilitation are so considerable that those who respect the law, who make it their duty to be citizens respectful of the freedom of others, are at times deprived of the money they would need to further assist the society in which they live.
I remember that not so long ago, in the case of a local initiative, I had strongly recommended the launching of two projects: Cinebec and the Conseil des parents. But these two projects have been turned down. Sometime, certain people in my riding-and I think that this is the same in others-say: You are spending $10,000 in order to try and rehabilitate a convict, and when some people submit respectable and honest projects, you refuse to grant them the required credits.
I think that it is time, if we want society to find again its fundamental values, as well as the wealth that has made it into what it is now, that policies tend toward greater assistance, for those who work modestly but honestly in our society. Those are the middle-class people, who see their taxes rising all the time. Those are also the aged who receive only $135 or $255 a month those who in fact are
May 1, 1972

the backbone of society, and who are too often neglected because of the wrong-doings of some people towards whom I do not want to be unjust because they are not always entirely responsible for their actions. Nevertheless they have violated the law and have acted towards society in such a way as to surely deserve some punishment.
Just the same, Mr. Speaker, I think that priorities should be set up sometimes. And I must say that the bill now being considered-this may be a source of hope for me, as I said earlier-includes excellent provisions which, in my opinion, are bound to be satisfactory to us.
For instance, when it is provided that a suicide attempt is no longer an offence under the law, I think that this is quite normal, and should have been enacted many years ago. In fact, people committing such an offence are obviously sick in their minds, and putting them in jail will never offer a solution to their problems. I think that anybody will agree on that.
Added to all this, there is a very good provision with which I am genuinely pleased. In my profession, I have often had to defend people charged with driving a car while under the influence of liquor. Their driving permits were taken away from them, and could no longer earn their living.
Today, the law has become more lenient because it considers that not only the one who infringes the law must be penalized in a certain way, but also that we must not deprive the family of its sole breadwinner. As a matter of fact, being deprived of his driving licence, the accused lost his job and was no longer able to earn his own living and that of his family. This provision of the law that allows an intermittent sentence is, in my view, a great improvement, and I think it will be well received by all the right-thinking people.
There is also the question of the National Parole Board. And on this point, I would be tempted to agree with the comments made by the hon. member who spoke before me. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we would not have to vote on the re-establishment of capital punishment if the National Parole Board was playing its role better. I believe it must be recognized-and I should like my criticism to be constructive-that all too often those who benefit most from this Board are the most hardened criminals. I have personally had the opportunity to defend cases where in my opinion the accused were worthy of consideration. They were first offenders soliciting parole to whom this privilege was denied. I knew on the other hand that hardened criminals, with heavy records, were able, by means unknown but deplored, to obtain parole and thereby returned to society where they committed new crimes which brought them back to jail.
I believe the Parole Board, which is an essential agency, should be restructured and that it should really fulfill the purpose for which it was created, parole being limited to cases where there is a real likelihood of rehabilitation.
The matter of capital punishment will, in my opinion, be much less serious and it should be easier for us to arrive at a decision in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, the Parole Board might be one of the most important problems but I trust that its efficiency will be improved in the not too distant future.
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
Mr. Speaker, I think that this bill which has been in preparation for nearly a year provides some solutions. For instance, I was favourably impressed by the comments of my friend the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth) this afternoon on the clause that provides that a judge after a trial or an admission of guilt can refrain from imposing a fine or a sentence of imprisonment on an individual who has pleaded guilty or has been declared guilty.
In my opinion, it is wrong to have the bill not prevent the individual from being convicted because if the person concerned does not deserve a conviction, I cannot see why he would deserve having a criminal record when one considers its importance and implications. In spite of the fact that the new Criminal Records Act provides for the destruction of a reocrd after a period of five years, during that time the record of an individual may be a millstone around his neck which limits his possibilities for employment and often excludes him from taking any active part in society.
I should have liked-I shall discuss this matter in committee-the bill to go still farther, because, some highly technical offences appear to have been committed. I remember, for instance, the case of this man who now has a criminal record because during a hunting season, he had kept in his locked car a loaded gun with both locks in the "safety" position. I find it highly ridiculous that this man's life be affected by a criminal record which may limit his activity and prevent him from playing an important part in society.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, puts an end to the use of the lash. I think that everybody agrees that corporal punishment is not a human way of making those people guilty of errors pay their debt to society. I think it is pointless to discuss it any further; we are happy for it. It does indicate that the government has made a step further, making a move for which the minister should be commended.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude these comments by saying: that this bill which is immensely important, must not lead us to forget that the Criminal Code, as it is, needs to be overhauled and I hope that the Law Reform Commission of Canada will enter into action as soon as possible, in order to propose a law better adjusted to our modern needs and written, I hope, in a clearer language.
People are often complaining and rightly so that the words used are often incomprehensible and that, in a certain way, they lead to injustice. I hope that the Law Reform Commission will accomplish its work in a competent and fair manner and that it will look for ways to improve the Criminal Code so that it will meet the present needs.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying a while ago, I hope that this proposed legislation which is excellent and which meets with my approval will not restrict the money put at the disposal of other honest and thoughtful citizens who are playing an active role in society and within the framework of the Youth Opportunities Program. I would hope that those who have submitted projects will not for ever be refused the money needed for the realization of their projects because it has been used for people other than those who really need it.

May 1, 1972

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a lawyer I feel it necessary to become involved in this debate. On the other hand, I do not wish to be repetitious because my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) has put before the House the position our party feels it should take. I think he should be commended for the argument he elaborated and placed before the House, because it showed a considerable amount of thought and a contemporary thinking. In all fairness to the government, I believe it is moving in the right direction in this regard also. I also find it extremely important to relate our social ills to crime because it seems to me they have been related for some time.
I believe it would be wrong for us to think that the bill which is before us amending several sections of the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, and so on, is a panacea for what one could call domestic tranquility, in terms of violence. I wish to place on record some thoughts I have garnered as a result of being in possession of an extremely important report tabled in 1969 by a commission in the United States.
In order to give some credibility to the statement I have just made, in terms of not being able to separate the two matters to which I referred, violence and our social ills, I recommend that members who were on the justice committee and those who would like to be enlightened, like my hon. friend on the left who always interjects-I hope he will give us an opportunity to hear his words of wisdom-acquire this report entitled, "The final report of the National Commission on the Causes and Prevention of Violence". The title indicates that some thought went into the inquiry because it also states it was to establish justice and to ensure domestic tranquility. I think this is the sort of thing we are all concerned about-domestic tranquility and the establishment of justice.
I hope hon. members will understand what I am hoping to point out when I refer to this question. I shall not dwell on it too long but shall merely give some concrete examples of why I have been able to come to the conclusion that we should not look on this bill as a panacea. I recommend this report to all members who do not have a copy of it. Hon. members who were part of the Canadian delegation met many of our colleagues in the United States and it would be very simple to write them and ask for a copy of this book. I believe it is extremely important to read what is stated in the book on page 27, as follows:
Much has been written about inner-city slums where crime and delinquency are bred. Social scientists have analyzed slum conditions and their causal link to crime and violence, writers and artists have dramatized the sordidness and the frustrations of life in the inner cities, and a number of Commissions prior to this one have produced comprehensive reports on this subject. In its 1967 report the Crime Commission described the linkage between violent crime and slum conditions in large cities as "one of the most fully documented facts about crime".
To interject briefly, may I say that what I mean by violence and crime as referred to in this report is primarily homicide, rape, assault and robbery. It continues:
Referring to numerous studies conducted over a period of years, the commission found that violent crime, its offenders and its victims are found most often in urban areas characterized by: low income, physical deterioration, dependency, racial and ethnic concentrations, broken homes, working mothers, low levels of education and vocational skills, high unemployment, high proportions of single males, overcrowded and substandard housing, low rates of home ownership or single family dwellings, mixed land use, high population density.
I think my point is well taken: it is very difficult to separate the reasons for a person's social behaviour from the reasons for the social ills which exist today. I give the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) some credit. He is new on the job, and most of this work was done by his predecessor, whom I also wish to compliment. A bill such as this does not enable us to get mean easily.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT

Sometimes I get carried away because I cannot understand how this government can ignore the problems and frustrations of people. However, since I am not supposed to be mean this evening, and I said I would not be mean, I give credit to the former minister of justice-perhaps I am taking this out of context-who said that the law shall never again stand still. Those are significant words. I hope it will never again stand still, because if it does we will unquestionably be faced with confrontation from those who believe that the administration of justice has no meaning for them and even this place has no meaning for them. I hope that the present Minister of Justice has taken a page from the former minister of justice when he stated:
In our day we can far less afford the delays which we have suffered in the past. It is more dangerous and less defensible to leave our legal system, our whole belief in the working of freedom, vulnerable to those who have a case against a particular rule when we have to agree with their case and should move to change the rule.
In other words, we are faced with change, not change for the sake of change but change which is necessary because of the contemporary way of thinking and the circumstances in which we live which lead to so much frustration. One thing about which I am pleased is that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, of which I am a member, is a highly respected committee. I think all hon. members will agree with this. We come from all parts of the country. Certainly we have different ideas, but among our group are to be found many lawyers. They do not pussyfoot when it comes to bills. We do not argue and we do not fight.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. 1972 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE, CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT, NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, PAROLE ACT AND VISITING FORCES ACT
speechtext:
The exception is you. I do not know whether there are too many lawyers, but what I am trying to say is that we have a high calibre of lawyer on the committee. They are intelligent and, generally speaking, non-partisan when dealing with bills such as this. When the Minister of Justice says that he hopes we will give this bill speedy passage and will bring before the committee amendments of some consequence, he can be sure the bill will receive that treatment. I have a feeling that the minister means what he says. If he is anything like the former minister of justice, we will get along quite well.
Here we have an omnibus bill amending the Criminal Code, the Criminal Code 1967 Amendment Act, the Criminal Records Act, the National Defence Act, the Parole Act and the Visiting Forces Act. In dealing with all these acts the government is attempting to remove certain offences and punishments. This is a commendable attitude because obviously certain offences should not be included in the Criminal Code, such as attempted suicide. It is high time we removed it. Generally speaking, we are dealing with social behaviour in contemporary society and occasions when governments should move in to deter conduct which Canadians as a whole find offensive and not in keeping with the type of society in which we would like to live.
As I understand it, there are some 75 clauses of significant magnitude affecting the acts to which I have just referred. Hopefully, when we are through with this bill it will become more meaningful. Hopefully, it will exhibit a need for change to rid our criminal law of an archaic climate, a law which is riddled with anomalies, one which for some time has had no new approaches and has not been responsive to the changing needs of our society.
I gave the former minister of justice credit for having indicated some time ago that the law will never again stand still. We are moving in the right direction in deliberating on this bill. As I said, this amendment will not be the panacea which we seek. The problems that all members of parliament face are difficult. However, there is a study that is being undertaken now. Perhaps we are moving too quickly with this bill, but on further deliberation I do not think we are because there are certain things that this bill will achieve and we cannot afford to wait for the conclusions of the law reform commission under the chairmahship of Mr. Justice E. Hartt. I refer to the removal from the Criminal Code of corporal punishment. It should have been removed some time ago. I think it is barbaric. It seems to me an attempt to seek vengeance upon the accused. I cannot see how corporal punishment could be a deterrent.
Today we have to face the crimes of skyjacking and air piracy which are reprehensible crimes. Surely we have to deal with them immediately and cannot afford to wait for what I am sure will be commendable conclusions and recommendations of the law reform commission. The law reform commission, in a publication entitled "Research Program I," has given some indication of the problems with which they are faced. I want to put it on the record. Perhaps hon. members do not know what they are
Criminal Law Amendment Act. 1972
attempting to do, what they are faced with and what their conclusions may be when they have finished their deliberations. I shall read from it quite extensively, though not to the point of boredom, for the benefit of hon. members who have not had an opportunity of looking at this issue. At page 12, under the heading "Aims and purposes of the criminal law" it reads:
At present there is confusion and controversy about the functions of the criminal law. Thus, the commission will study on a continuing basis the purposes to be served by the criminal law in our Canadian society. In particular, we will be concerned with: identifying the types of conduct which should be made subject to the criminal law; analysing the objectives to be attained by the imposition of criminal sanctions; finding alternative techniques for regulating conduct without resorting to the criminal law; studying the effectiveness of the adversary system; and examining the existing classification of offences and the jurisdiction of the courts.
The most important statement that I take out of this is that here is the law reform commission, which is headed by one of Canada's leading jurists, indicating that at present the criminal law is in an area of confusion and controversy about its functions. Under the heading, "General principles of criminal law" it reads:
The commission will study the general principles common to most offences with a view to their clarification and codification. Many of these principles are not now contained in the Criminal Code but are developed through statutory interpretation and judge-made law. As a result, there is uncertainty about some of the fundamental issues of criminal law. The study will include in the initial stages: the mental elements of the offence; strict responsibility; ignorance and mistake of fact and law; mental illness; intoxication; compulsion and necessity; extra-territorial extent of the criminal law; and corporate criminal culpability.
Another part of the program which the commission will delve into is described as, "The attainment of equality before the law." It reads:
The commission will study the impact of the criminal law on specialized groups within society to determine whether it is operating equitably. Special studies will be undertaken into the problems of the native offender and poverty and the criminal law.
That is a commendable program and I will deal with it a little later. Under the heading, "Prohibited and regulated conduct" it reads:
The commission will study offences now contained or that should be contained in the Criminal Code with a view to the enactment of a comprehensive code reflecting contemporary values.
I would like to so pause there, Mr. Speaker. It is too bad this type of commission has not been operating for five years so that we could have the benefit of its wisdom. I think we are a little premature in introducing this bill when we know that we now have a law reform commission which will be studying in depth this area of criminal law. But because of the necessity for passing a number of important clauses of the bill, we must move ahead with it. I continue to quote:
Some of the questions to be explored for each offence are: whether the conduct should be prohibited by law; whether the criminal process is the best technique for controlling that conduct; whether the physical and mental elements of the offence have been defined with sufficient certainty and in a rational and understandable manner; and whether the penalty set out in the statute for the offence is realistic. The matters to be studied and reported on at

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972
an early stage are: homicide; sexual misconduct; obscenity; contempt; conspiracy; and dishonest acquisition of property.
Mr. Speaker, what we are doing now is certainly a step in the right direction, but the problem is extremely complex, calling for more than the standing committee on justice to delve into this bill. It calls for expertise and for hearings to be held around the country, something which I understand the law reform commission will be doing so that it may have the advice not only of jurists and administrators but of other persons who are affected by the criminal law.
One of the matters the commission will be looking at is homicide. Right now, homicide and the penalty for homicide constitute a burning question. I was not here five years ago when capital punishment was debated with deep conviction by members on all sides of the House. I understand there was a free vote taken on the issue. But as I have thought of the matter over the years, particularly since becoming a member of this House knowing that we would again have to face the issue, I have always wondered whether capital punishment in fact is a deterrent and whether it is morally right.
What disturbs me is not so much the answers to those two questions but the answer to this one: Can we make a mistake? Here I am really in a quandary. I know what the pressures are. If somebody says to me, "Let us bring back capital punishment because these are the statistics," I will reply, "Everybody knows what can be done with statistics." But what is unfortunate with respect to the law as it stands is that it was supposed to have been a five-year experiment and has turned out not to be an experiment at all.
Apparently members of this House, on a free vote, decided that capital punishment should be abolished except in the case of the murder of a prison guard or policeman. What has been the result? Policemen have been slain, and I have always been asked the question, "What goes on? I thought you chaps passed a law five years ago providing capital punishment for the murder of a policeman." I really did not know the answer myself but I knew there was an answer to the question. Then I found out that the answer was that when parliament passed this law it never did away with the prerogative of the cabinet to commute the death sentence. This is what the average person does not realize. He forgets that the cabinet has power to commute the death sentence. The result is that we have a law that is not a law.
I am not trying to be partisan this evening, but here we have a cabinet going against the wishes of the elected representatives of the people who wanted a five-year experiment. That is why we are in the present quandary. That is why the Canadian people are so upset. That is why they do not know what the law really is. They apparently believe that if a policeman or guard is slain, then the killer should face the maximum penalty.
There was a debate of some significance on this question five years ago. Why in heaven's name have we not followed the law? Had we done so we might now have the solution to a very burning question, a determination of the pros and cons regarding the abolition of capital punishment. The government has left the Canadian people in a dilemma. The government should have had the compas-

sion either to wipe out the law or abide by the law as it stands. I can live with and accept the law as it stands now and, as I said before, I have to reach a happy balance between it and those who are involved with the protection of lives and property, our policemen and prison guards. As the law stands now, they will say this is discrimination. Perhaps it is. But I have to answer the question that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon told us to ask ourselves: What if we make a mistake?
I will be very frank, Mr. Speaker. Apparently most lawyers around here have been involved as counsel in about 20 murder cases, and many give the impression that they are the greatest counsel that ever lived. I took part in only one murder trial and I do not particularly want to be involved in any more. The pressure that was exerted on me was enormous, not only with respect to my capabilities as a lawyer but because I thought that if the jury was not of a high calibre, and because of my inadequacies in going through the appeal procedure, this man might hang. I was bothered then and still am. As far as I am concerned, let somebody else who has the fortitude and strength, and who can go to bed when the case is over and forget about it, conduct murder trials. I see the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Deakon) looking at me. He knows what I am talking about. I can live with this law because it is provided that the government will move in the right direction and do what it is told to do, forget about commuting sentences.
Mr. Speaker, all countries are concerned about this problem. I shall put just a few statistics on the record. In several major countries the death penalty has been abolished by law: Argentina, Australia-Queensland and New South Wales-Brazil, Great Britain, Colombia, Costa Rica, Denmark, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, West Germany, Finland, Greenland, Iceland, Italy, Mexico-25 of 29 states-Norway, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and many of the states in the United States of America. That is why we shall have to deal with this problem. I may have to change my mind six months from now, and I want help in this regard. I am not concerned about whether it is morally right or whether there is a deterrent; what bothers me is that a court and a jury may make a mistake and send an innocent man to the gallows.
In New Zealand, capital punishment was abolished in 1941. In 1951, it was reinstated and in 1956 the death penalty was again abolished although it was not formally removed from the statutes until 1961. The minister of justice for New Zealand made this statement during the course of parliamentary debates in 1961:
When we realize that the penalty for murder has changed three times in the period I have been reviewing-in 1935, in 1950 and 1957-with no effect on the figures; then surely it is plain to us that executing murderers does not achieve anything.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, that is the problem we are faced with. There was one particular program within the objectives of the law reform commission that struck home. I want to spend a few minutes on it because I think it is extremely important. I refer to the attainment of equality before the courts. Most judges are impartial,
May 1, 1972

have a sense of responsibility and accept the fact that this country is a multicultural society with people of different races, creeds, colours and religion contributing to the quality of our life. But there are still some judges who for some reason or other make derogatory statements not only to the detriment of the accused but to the detriment of the group to which the accused belongs.
Mr. Speaker, I thought I was making a pretty good speech, but when I hear the noise in this House I wonder. I do not want members to stop talking while I am making a speech, but to just tone it down a little.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak briefly on this bill. I was also pleased to listen to the fine speech made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). There are times in one's political life when one feels close to brother members of parliament. This sense of closeness transcends ideologies. The present occasion is an example of that sort of spirit which has arisen in the House because, Mr. Speaker, those who believe in the rule of law cannot oppose these amendments to the Criminal Code.
The bill covers everything that happens to an accused from the time he is arrested until he is convicted and punished. The whole bill is a compromise between humanity, in some parts, and growing severity in others. It shows more humanity in crimes such as common assault where previously a person could be convicted of an indictable offence. It will no longer be possible to treat common assault as an indictable offence. A charge of common assault usually arises when someone loses his

May 1, 1972
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1972 cool and makes a fool of himself. A man like that will be treated with compassion.
At the same time, the bill deals more severely with assault occasioning bodily harm, the maximum sentence for which is to be increased to five years. Under the code as it is at present, cases involving extreme violence were inadequately dealt with. The maximum sentence of two years was inadequate. I think a better balance has been struck in the law, lesser penalties will be meted out for lesser offences and more severe penalties for more severe offences.
I am glad that it will be possible for one to appeal a conviction for contempt of court. It was manifestly unjust, I think, that previously a judge had the power to convict a criminal or even counsel and that the law did not give either of them the right to appeal. This appeal provision is a major step forward in our law and all will recognize it as modern and humanitarian.
The question of public mischief is dealt with. I agree with the maximum sentence of five years. The offence may also be dealt with on summary conviction. That provision is good. A court can deal with people of low intelligence by way of summary conviction. On the other hand, of course, serious cases can be proceeded with by way of indictment. All in all, I think that justice will be done as it should be done.
There is in the bill a provision that concerns jurors. It overcomes previous weaknesses in the law. Previously, a judge was not empowered to dismiss a juror unless he was satisfied that it was impossible for the juror to continue serving. He might have been suffering a great deal of pain and might not have been discharged. Now it is provided that if in the opinion of the judge there is good reason for the juror not to continue serving, the juror may be discharged and his services dispensed with.
The bill is full of humanitarian reforms. In places it patches the law; in others it makes humane provision with respect to records, whether convictions will be allowed to stand, and whether a conditional discharge will be allowed. The entire subject of the bill will be dealt with in committee. I am proud to be a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which will review these matters in detail.
I cannot refrain from speaking about the wording of section 309, printed at page 18 of the bill, dealing with possession of housebreaking instruments under suspicious circumstances. I will not go into details now, but it seems to me that under this section the court is saddled with three burdens of proof whereas one burden is usually enough. First, there is the overriding burden of proof resting on the Crown, which must prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. Then an onus is cast on an accused, who must deal with the matter. Then an onus seems to be cast on the Crown. I think these burdens of proof should be spelled out in more detail.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak about two aspects of the legislation before the House which have concerned me particularly since 1967. Earlier today reference was made to the leadership given by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) to the movement for abolishing corporal punishment and to

the work that the parliamentary committee did in the mid-1950s. It has taken remarkably long for those concerned with the furtherance of justice to implement previous recommendations and bring about the abolishment of corporal punishment.
The term corporal punishment is often misunderstood. When people talk about corporal punishment they think they are talking about hanging. It has nothing to do with hanging. Corporal punishment means the use of the whip or strap, an instrument of punishment previously in common use. It was imposed after criminals had been convicted of certain offences and sent to federal institutions. In recent years this form of punishment has been used less and less. Now, in introducing this law reform, the minister is merely making regular what has become standard and accepted practice. To be honest, let me say that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), by including this measure in the bill is taking a greater risk than if he had introduced it two or three years ago. A growing number of people in this country think it is useful to retain this anachronistic and revengeful form of punishment known as corporal punishment.
I see my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. Later in this debate I shall say why it is important to abolish corporal punishment once and for all. May I call it ten o'clock?

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-LARGER INCREASE IN FOOD COSTS IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-REFERENCE TO PRICES AND INCOMES COMMISSION
speechtext:
In baseball, Mr. Speaker, after three strikes you're out. I hope that does not apply to me, for this is the third time I have spoken today.
In bringing this matter to the attention of the House I am raising something that has been the concern of hon. members representing Prince Edward Island, and of the Premier of Prince Edward Island for the past few months. The matter was initially raised in correspondence among members of this House representing Prince Edward Island constituencies, the Premier of Prince Edward Island and Statistics Canada.
I think all Canadians in the last two or three years have been alarmed by rapidly rising food costs. From time to time the complaints of housewives, the most important body in the country, reach the ears of representatives in legislative chambers. We heard such complaints four years ago when the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) chaired, with Senator Croll, that important committee investigating the alarming and rapid increase in food costs.
In talking about the subject of high food costs I want to focus strictly on the situation as it pertains to Prince
May 1, 1972

Edward Island. I want to do this because I think a myth has grown in this country which suggests that it is cheaper to live in places like Prince Edward Island and other areas with a relatively low standard of living and low income. When federal wage scales are set or when federal estimates are made on the amount of expenditures necessary to establish comparable levels of equality of income, it is often concluded that a person can live more cheaply in a place such as Prince Edward Island or the Maritimes generally than in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver.
One might almost call this the Judy LaMarsh myth. Perhaps it is not fair to refer to the hon. lady because she is no longer a member of this chamber. I remember a famous occasion when she was speaking in Ontario. She said that an old age pensioner could live much more cheaply in Prince Edward Island than in Ontario. I hope the hon. lady is listening, and others who still cherish that myth. I have facts to indicate that in one of the most vital areas in terms of consumer costs, food, this is unfortunately not the case.

The hon. member has suggested rents. I hope we will have an opportunity to discuss that subject on another occasion. It is also an important and related question. There is also the matter of transportation and fuel costs. However, this evening I am focusing on food costs. I have received figures from Statistics Canada which go into some detail. I think it is important to place them on the record. In January, 1969, starting with the $1 figure in Charlottetown, Saint John and Halifax, the criteria was established as to how much $1 would buy. Running through to the end of 1969, food costs showed an increase in those three Maritime centres that was roughly comparable. In December, 1969, food costs had risen to 103.8 in Charlottetown, 104 in Saint John and 104.8 in Halifax.
To the end of 1970 there was a very slight increase in Charlottetown to 104.4. There was a decrease in Saint John to 100.1, and in Halifax to 99.6. I now come to the alarming part. In 1971 there was a rapid rise in food costs in Charlottetown from 105.8 in January to 111.3 in December of that year. In Saint John there was an increase from 100.6 to 106.4 and in Halifax from 99.8 to 103.8. One can see the alarming rate of increase that took place in Charlottetown in the year 1971. While there was a similar increase in the other Maritime centres, it was obviously not as big. In 1972 the cost jumped from 111.7 in January to 113.5 in February, and 113.9 in March-almost 114. In Saint John the figure went from 106.3 in January to 108.2 in March, and in Halifax from 104.8 in January to 105.4 in March. This rapid rise in costs has to be treated very seriously. I think that on a statistical basis people are aware of the way in which they are paying a great deal more for their food.
The answers are not simple but they are at least clear. The issue of transportation has to be the basic one. The issue of transportation to and from the Island has been one that successive governments since confederation have avoided. As a result, almost all the commodities on the island originating from mainland Canada cost more. Almost all the commodities, basic foodstuffs that we sell

Order. I regret that the time of the hon. member has expired.
Mr. ]udd Buchanan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has indicated, Statistics Canada has looked into the situation in Prince Edward Island and found that the trend of food prices in Charlottetown and Halifax has been sharply different in the two places since 1969. It appears clear that an anomalous situation exists there.
As suggested by the hon. member, it may well be that part of this problem arises from transportation costs, and the extra costs involved are certainly a factor in food prices. However, the most important factor may well be the degree of retail competition in different areas. The large retail chains are heavily dependent on traffic in the large urban centres and competition is usually very keen.
In contrast, the attitude of merchants in smaller centres is frequently somewhat more relaxed. This does not imply that any conspiracy is involved, but merely that they are not forced by the market situation to compete as vigorously as they are in the larger centres. This would seem to be part of the problem in Charlottetown. The so-called food price war which began in 1970 did not, it seems, extend to Charlottetown nor, let us be candid, to a great many other parts of Canada.
Food prices, as the hon. member has mentioned, are the most visible of the prices paid by ordinary consumers and also have the greatest impact on public attitudes toward inflation. It would provide a more balanced view of the situation if account could be taken of the prices of a much wider range of goods and services. Although we do not have any precise information on the subject, it is probable that some of the disadvantages to the outlying areas in terms of food prices are counterbalanced by lower accommodation and service costs.
We should probably focus more attention on the over-all standard of living in different regions. It would seem that we should be striving for greater equality in standards of living and that we should accept disparities in particular price levels provided that similar groups of people in different areas have roughly equivalent living standards which they are able to enjoy.

Mr. Speaker, about five years ago the federal government commissioned two University of British Columbia professors, Professor Stan-bury and Professor Fields, to make a study of taxation in the broadest possible sense as it related to Indian people in that province. As far as I can gather, the federal government paid the whole shot for that study; it was a federal government examination and survey.

The Stanbury-Fields report, as it became known, was subsequently concluded and presented to the federal government. On a number of occasions I have moved motions in the House asking that that report be made public; in other words, be tabled. At first when these motions of mine were put forward a few years ago, the government objected to them on the ground that the report was of a confidential nature and could not be disclosed. In fact, I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Laing) was minister of Indian affairs at the time I first raised the question. At any rate, the federal government indicated it could not disclose this report because it was confidential. But we persisted in our requests.
A couple of years ago this government acquiesced and said in effect, "We have examined the report. We do not consider it to be confidential, so we will agree to table it subject to permission of the province of British Columbia." The province of B.C. subsequently denied that permission and the report was not tabled. I submit that inasmuch as it was a federal report related to a subject matter coming exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada, namely, Indian people, and inasmuch as it was financed entirely out of federal revenue, the province of British Columbia has no position whatsoever in this matter, permission should not have been asked for nor should the denial of the province have been heeded at that time.
That report makes some very interesting disclosures about the position of Indian people, the amount of taxes they pay and the fact that they are cheated regarding their land tax position, in that reserve land is leased to the province of British Columbia. They are being cheated by the provincial government and I suggest that is the reason the province does not want the report tabled.
I suggest that the House did pass a motion to the effect that this report be tabled and I now seek permission to table four chapters of it, being the part I have been able to obtain. Mr. Speaker, pursuant to a motion this House passed, I ask permission to table chapters 7, 9, 10 and 11 of the Stanbury-Fields report.

Mr. )udd Buchanan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, in 1967 the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development engaged the services of Professor D. B. Fields of the faculty of commerce and business administration, University of British Columbia, to undertake a study and quantitative assessment of the status of Indians as taxpayers in the province of British Columbia. The project shall consist of a study and quantitative assessment of the financial significance of the special status of Indians as taxpayers in the province of British Columbia and without limiting its scope in any way shall include a general analysis of present and potential taxes levied on Indians, the nature and cost of services rendered to Indians at present and future trends, the growing significance of taxes paid by non-Indian leaseholders of

maintopic: TRANSPORT-UPDATING OF YEAR OF MANUFACTURE OF FOREIGN AUTOMOBILES-ACTION TO END PRACTICE.
TRANSPORT-UPDATING OF YEAR OF MANUFACTURE OF FOREIGN AUTOMOBILES-ACTION TO END PRACTICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 28 last I raised a question with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) regarding the updating of certain automobiles, mainly imported automobiles. This is a topic which has excited a considerable amount of interest across the nation and one to which I believe the government should direct its attention. I realize there is a dual responsibility here and that probably the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andras) has just as keen an interest in the matter as his colleague the Minister of Transport.
The question has many ramifications. As I say, it has excited a great deal of interest across the nation. Apart from the fact that the Department of Transport certainly has a legitimate interest in this topic as a result of the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, the department I think should be prepared to answer a few questions and take a more direct interest in what is going on. For example, I should like to know how many people within the Department of Transport deal directly with questions concerning automobile safety.
I should also like to know how many complaints are registered annually with the department on this subject, and what sanctions are available through the Department of Transport to enforce regulations pertaining to auto safety and registration procedures. There is a real problem here so far as consumers are concerned because at this time, due to Canada's status as what has been called a dumping ground for unsafe and misregistered vehicles, any vehicle, I am informed, may be arbitrarily registered by the auto maker in any year desired, with full government approval. The only problem is that no one bothers to tell the consumer about this. Then he buys a new 1972 Datsun, Toyota or Volvo, for example, he may find much to his surprise that what he really bought is last year's model.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Most customers only discover the error when they return to their dealer the next year and find that their car has depreciated perhaps by two years, with a depreciation factor of 50 per cent rather than the expected 30 per cent. By this the motorist learns to his sorrow that he has paid more for his insurance, that his car's rusting is normal rather than premature, and that most sales contracts have a clause which prohibits him from doing much about it.
Aside from financial loss suffered, these redated automobiles pose a serious safety hazard. Certain 1971 and 1972 models advertised as incorporating the latest federally-controlled safety devices may in fact be substandard in construction, because the Canada Motor Vehicle Safety Act is effective only for vehicles manufactured after January, 1971, and normally any car registered as a 1972 vehicle would incorporate the features specified in the Canada Motor Vehicle Safety Act. However, this is not always the case and the motorist loses a great deal financially and so far as his personal well-being is concerned.
There is another point which is of concern. I suppose the import tax collected on foreign automobiles is predicated to some extent on the year they were manufactured. If there is some uncertainty as to the status of the vehicles allowed into the country and the fact that they may be updated, as it sometimes appears may well be the case, then I think the amount of import tax collected would be affected. If such is the case, I urge the government to look into this aspect of the matter.
There is another problem involving registration. I should like to quote from a submission made by a responsible consumer group in which the following statement appears:
Mr. Karl Barths, president of Volkswagen Canada Limited, recently told two members of the APA executive staff that Volkswagen had a serious problem in the early sixties with the now famous "grey market" selling of Volkswagens. Old Volkswagens were updated and sold to unsuspecting American motorists. This fraud was quickly ended, however, when Volkswagen of America improved its serial numbering system in 1965 so that anyone could determine when the car was built.
If that could be done at the initiative of the Americans, surely the Canadian government could double-check to see whether something like that could not be done here. I realize that time is a factor and I would conclude by suggesting that there are certain things that the Department of Transport and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs could do. I make the suggestion because there are few things that interest the average Canadian as much as his automobile, and if he feels that something is phony about the way imported cars are being sold in the country, or for that matter any car, it will have a detrimental effect on the industry as a whole.
It seems to me that the import car industry in particular should be forced to set up machinery for a just rebate system for dealers who are left with old unsold models; that all car serial numbers should be filed with federal and provincial departments of consumer affairs and that complete reimbursement for all valid consumer claims, equal to the monetary difference between the real and the fictional age of the vehicle, should be instituted.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Recently the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs held a press conference in Montreal at which he dealt with this problem. That is why I said at the beginning of my remarks that this is really a dual responsibility, but a governmental responsibility nevertheless. At that press conference a certain amount of attention was paid to the proposition that assistance would be available to consumers who wished to institute suits as a result of grievances which they suffered at the hands of dealers of imported cars. I would like to know what has been done in this regard, how many suits have been instituted, whether the government is really concerned about the problem or whether this is just a convenient way to dispose of it.

Mr. Speaker, following a question asked in this House on March 28 by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) concerning current regulations on motor vehicle safety, I indicated in a written reply tabled on April 26 that any vehicle manufactured or imported in Canada after January 1, 1971, had to bear a label showing the month and year of manufacture.
The Minister of Transport feels he has a duty to ensure that vehicles meet requirements concerning the conformity label prescribed by the regulations on motor vehicle
safety, and a signed declaration for each vehicle is required of all importers.
Moreover, the records of manufacturers and importers are examined, and vehicles are inspected at customs offices in ports of entry as well as at the importers'. Whenever a complaint is received from the public, an investigation is made, and finally, the operations of manufacturers in Canada are under constant supervision.
One must also take into account the fact that any person who violates the Motor Vehicle Safety Act is liable, on summary conviction, to a fine ranging from $1,000 to $10,000 or, on conviction by way of indictment, to a fine from $5,000 to $200,000, whether the offence is committed by a private person or a corporation.
The hon. member must be aware of the press release that was issued by the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) on April 24, and I guess he will be able to look into it if he has not done so yet, because he will find there all the information he wants about the subject matter we are dealing with tonight.

I also have taken note of other points of interest brought forward by the hon. member. I shall inform the minister of them in order to provide the hon. member with all necessary information.
